options.B: Minutes entered WITHIN 30 DAYS of conclusion of meeting; SEPARATE MINUTE BOOKS for each type (general meetings, Board meetings, each committee); pages consecutively numbered; fair and correct summary; each page initialled/signed; last page dated and signed — general meeting: Chairman within 30 days; Board/committee: Chairman of that meeting or next; preserved PERMANENTLY at registered office; MINUTE BOOKS = EVIDENCE of proceedings
options.C: Minutes can be kept anywhere; no specific time limit for entry
options.D: Minutes are optional — only formal resolutions need to be recorded

answer_html:
Answer: (C) Minutes can be kept anywhere; no specific time limit for entry

Rule 25 / Section 118: MINUTES RULES: (1) SEPARATE MINUTE BOOK for each type: GENERAL MEETINGS, BOARD MEETINGS, and EACH COMMITTEE; (2) ENTRY WITHIN 30 DAYS of conclusion of meeting; POSTAL BALLOT: brief report entered within 30 days of passing resolution; (3) Pages CONSECUTIVELY NUMBERED; each page INITIALLED/SIGNED; (4) LAST PAGE DATED AND SIGNED: General meeting — by CHAIRMAN WITHIN 30 DAYS (or director authorised by Board on death/inability); Board/Committee — by Chairman of that meeting or next meeting; Postal ballot — by Chairman of Board within 30 days; (5) Minutes = EVIDENCE of proceedings; meeting DEEMED DULY HELD and all proceedings duly taken; (6) Preserved PERMANENTLY at registered office; custody of CS or director authorised by Board.

question_html: Under Section 118(11) and (12), what are the PENALTIES for default in complying with minutes provisions and for TAMPERING with minutes?

options.A: MINUTES DEFAULT [Sec.118(11)]: Company = RS. 25,000; every defaulting officer = RS. 5,000; TAMPERING WITH MINUTES [Sec.118(12)]: imprisonment up to 2 YEARS AND fine NOT LESS THAN RS. 25,000 but may extend to RS. 1 LAKH
options.B: Both defaults: fine up to Rs. 1 lakh each
options.C: Tampering with minutes: only civil penalty
options.D: Minutes default: imprisonment only; tampering: fine only

answer_html:
Answer: (A) MINUTES DEFAULT [Sec.118(11)]: Company = RS. 25,000; every defaulting officer = RS. 5,000; TAMPERING WITH MINUTES [Sec.118(12)]: imprisonment up to 2 YEARS AND fine NOT LESS THAN RS. 25,000 but may extend to RS. 1 LAKH

MINUTES PENALTIES: Section 118(11): DEFAULT IN COMPLYING WITH MINUTES PROVISIONS: COMPANY = liable to penalty of RS. 25,000; EVERY DEFAULTING OFFICER = liable to penalty of RS. 5,000. Section 118(12): TAMPERING WITH MINUTES: Person found guilty = punishable with IMPRISONMENT for a term up to 2 YEARS AND FINE NOT LESS THAN RS. 25,000 but which may extend to RS. 1 LAKH. The serious penalty for tampering (including imprisonment) reflects the importance of minutes as authentic records of corporate decisions. Minutes are evidence of proceedings — tampering undermines corporate governance.

question_html: Under Section 119, what are the INSPECTION RIGHTS for minute books of general meetings?

options.A: Open to inspection by any person on payment of Rs. 100
options.B: Minute books of GENERAL MEETINGS at registered office; OPEN TO ANY MEMBER WITHOUT CHARGE — during business hours (NOT LESS THAN 2 HOURS per business day) subject to reasonable restrictions; COPIES within 7 WORKING DAYS on payment; INSPECTION REFUSED/COPY NOT FURNISHED: Company = RS. 25,000; defaulting officer = RS. 5,000
options.C: Only the Managing Director can inspect minute books
options.D: Minute books are confidential — no inspection rights for members

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Minute books of GENERAL MEETINGS at registered office; OPEN TO ANY MEMBER WITHOUT CHARGE — during business hours (NOT LESS THAN 2 HOURS per business day) subject to reasonable restrictions; COPIES within 7 WORKING DAYS on payment; INSPECTION REFUSED/COPY NOT FURNISHED: Company = RS. 25,000; defaulting officer = RS. 5,000

Section 119(1): Minute books of GENERAL MEETINGS and POSTAL BALLOT RESOLUTIONS kept at REGISTERED OFFICE and OPEN FOR INSPECTION by any MEMBER WITHOUT CHARGE during business hours, subject to such REASONABLE RESTRICTIONS as company may by articles or general meeting impose — NOT LESS THAN 2 HOURS IN EACH BUSINESS DAY for inspection. COPIES: Member entitled to COPY within 7 WORKING DAYS of request on payment of prescribed fees. PENALTY for inspection refusal or non-supply of copy: COMPANY = RS. 25,000 PENALTY; EVERY DEFAULTING OFFICER = RS. 5,000 FOR EACH REFUSAL OR DEFAULT. REPORT OF AGM, SPECIAL BUSINESS & MISCELLANEOUS — SECTIONS 102, 112, 121

question_html: Under Section 102, which of the following business transacted at an AGM is deemed ORDINARY BUSINESS (not requiring an explanatory statement)?

options.A: At AGM — ORDINARY BUSINESS: Consideration of FINANCIAL STATEMENTS and reports of Board and auditors; DECLARATION OF DIVIDEND; APPOINTMENT OF DIRECTORS retiring by rotation; APPOINTMENT OF AND FIXING REMUNERATION OF AUDITORS — ALL OTHER AGM business is deemed SPECIAL; ALL EGM business is deemed SPECIAL
options.B: All AGM business is deemed ordinary
options.C: Only resolutions for merger and acquisition are deemed special
options.D: None — all AGM business requires explanatory statement

answer_html:
Answer: (C) Only resolutions for merger and acquisition are deemed special

Section 102(2): At AGM, the following are ORDINARY BUSINESS (deemed): (1) Consideration of FINANCIAL STATEMENTS and REPORTS OF BOARD AND AUDITORS; (2) DECLARATION OF ANY DIVIDEND; (3) APPOINTMENT OF DIRECTORS in place of those RETIRING; (4) APPOINTMENT OF AND FIXING OF REMUNERATION OF AUDITORS. All OTHER BUSINESS at AGM and ALL BUSINESS at any other meeting = DEEMED SPECIAL. Special business requires an EXPLANATORY STATEMENT (Sec.102(1)) setting out material facts, nature of concern/interest of directors/managers/KMP/relatives, and other information to enable members to make informed decisions. Section 102(5): Default in Sec.102 — fine up to RS. 50,000 or 5 TIMES THE BENEFIT ACCRUED (whichever is more) for promoter/director/manager/KMP.
topic_text: Section 102 — Explanatory Statement & Deemed Special Business

question_html: Under Section 121 and Rule 31, what are the requirements for the REPORT OF THE AGM?

options.A: Report filed in FORM MGT-15 WITHIN 30 DAYS of conclusion of AGM; signed by CHAIRMAN or if unable to sign: TWO DIRECTORS (one being MD if any) + COMPANY SECRETARY; contains day/date/hour/venue, quorum, number of members attending, compliance confirmation, business transacted and results, adjournments — PREPARED IN ADDITION TO (not a substitute for) the MINUTES
options.B: Report of AGM is optional — only minutes are mandatory
options.C: Report filed within 60 days in Form MGT-7
options.D: Report signed only by the Chairman — no other signatures required

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Report filed in FORM MGT-15 WITHIN 30 DAYS of conclusion of AGM; signed by CHAIRMAN or if unable to sign: TWO DIRECTORS (one being MD if any) + COMPANY SECRETARY; contains day/date/hour/venue, quorum, number of members attending, compliance confirmation, business transacted and results, adjournments — PREPARED IN ADDITION TO (not a substitute for) the MINUTES

Rule 31 / Section 121: REPORT OF AGM: (1) FORM: MGT-15; (2) FILING: with Registrar WITHIN 30 DAYS of conclusion of AGM along with fee; (3) SIGNATORIES: CHAIRMAN of the meeting OR in case of inability: TWO DIRECTORS (one being MD if any) AND COMPANY SECRETARY; (4) CONTENTS: Day/date/hour/venue; confirmation of Chairman appointment; NUMBER OF MEMBERS ATTENDING; QUORUM CONFIRMATION; compliance with Act/Rules/Secretarial Standards; BUSINESS TRANSACTED AND RESULTS; particulars of any ADJOURNMENT/POSTPONEMENT/CHANGE IN VENUE; any other relevant points; (5) IMPORTANT: Report prepared IN ADDITION TO MINUTES (not a substitute); must contain a FAIR AND CORRECT SUMMARY of proceedings.

question_html: Under Sections 112 and 113, which of the following correctly states the right of representation at company meetings?

options.A: Sec.112: PRESIDENT or GOVERNOR (if member) may appoint any person as REPRESENTATIVE at any meeting — person deemed to be a MEMBER and entitled to same rights including RIGHT TO VOTE BY PROXY AND POSTAL BALLOT; Sec.113: BODY CORPORATE (member or creditor including debenture holder) may authorise REPRESENTATIVE with same rights as body corporate including RIGHT TO VOTE BY PROXY AND POSTAL BALLOT
options.B: Only the President of India can appoint a representative
options.C: Body corporates cannot appoint representatives
options.D: Representatives of President/Governors cannot vote at meetings

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Only the President of India can appoint a representative

Section 112: PRESIDENT OF INDIA or GOVERNOR OF A STATE, if a member of the company, may appoint any person he thinks fit as his REPRESENTATIVE at any meeting of the company or any class meeting. Such representative: DEEMED TO BE A MEMBER; entitled to exercise SAME RIGHTS AND POWERS including RIGHT TO VOTE BY PROXY AND POSTAL BALLOT as the President or Governor could exercise. Section 113: Where a BODY CORPORATE is a MEMBER OR CREDITOR (including debenture holder) — it may authorise any person as its REPRESENTATIVE at any meeting or class meeting or meeting of creditors. Such representative entitled to exercise SAME RIGHTS AND POWERS as the body corporate — including RIGHT TO VOTE BY PROXY AND POSTAL BALLOT. CONSOLIDATED ANSWER KEY — ALL 25 QUESTIONS — END OF QUESTION PAPER — Prepared from ICMAI Study Module | Management and Administration | Companies Act, 2013 — Sections 96–121 | Module 12.1 | Syllabus 2022 | CMA Inter June 2026
topic_text: Sections 112, 113 — Representation of President, Governors & Corporations

question_html: Under Section 13 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, a 'negotiable instrument' is defined as:

options.A: Any document that evidences a contractual right to payment and can be transferred
options.B: Any written instrument signed by the maker or drawer
options.C: A promissory note, bill of exchange, or cheque payable either to order or to bearer
options.D: Any commercial document used in trade and commerce

answer_html:
Answer: (C) A promissory note, bill of exchange, or cheque payable either to order or to bearer

Section 13: A NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENT is a PROMISSORY NOTE, BILL OF EXCHANGE, OR CHEQUE — payable either to ORDER or to BEARER. Indian law recognises only these THREE instruments as negotiable instruments. These instruments can transfer a better title to the holder — unlike ordinary documents. The NI Act was enacted in 1881 and is the primary law governing these instruments.

question_html: Under Section 4 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, a 'promissory note' is defined as an instrument in writing containing an unconditional undertaking, signed by the maker, to pay a certain sum of money only to, or to the order of, a certain person, or to the bearer of the instrument. Which of the following is NOT a promissory note?

options.A: 'I promise to pay B or order Rs. 50,000'
options.B: 'I promise to pay Rs. 20,000 seven days after my marriage with Helen'
options.C: 'I acknowledge myself to be indebted to B for Rs. 1 lakh to be paid on demand, for value received'
options.D: 'I promise to pay B the sum of Rs. 10,000 on 1st January 2026'

answer_html:
Answer: (B) 'I promise to pay Rs. 20,000 seven days after my marriage with Helen'

Section 4: A promissory note must contain an UNCONDITIONAL undertaking. 'I promise to pay Rs. 20,000 seven days after my marriage with Helen' is CONDITIONAL on marriage happening — hence NOT a promissory note. Similarly, 'I promise to pay Rs. 50,000 on D's death, provided D leaves me enough' — conditional and not a valid promissory note. Options A, C, and D are valid promissory notes.

question_html: In a promissory note, how many parties are there and what are they called?

options.A: Two parties — Maker (payer) and Payee
options.B: Three parties — Drawer, Drawee and Payee
options.C: Three parties — Maker, Acceptor and Payee
options.D: Two parties — Drawer and Drawee

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Two parties — Maker (payer) and Payee

Section 4: A PROMISSORY NOTE has TWO PARTIES: (1) the MAKER — the person who makes/signs the note and promises to pay; and (2) the PAYEE — the person to whom the payment is to be made. There is NO drawee in a promissory note (unlike a bill of exchange or cheque which have three parties). A promissory note cannot be self-drawn.

question_html: Under Section 5 of the NI Act, a 'bill of exchange' is an instrument in writing containing an UNCONDITIONAL ORDER, signed by the maker, directing a certain person to pay a certain sum of money to, or to the order of, a certain person or to the bearer. How many parties are there in a bill of exchange?

options.A: Two parties — Maker and Payee
options.B: Two parties — Drawer and Acceptor
options.C: Three parties — Drawer, Drawee/Acceptor and Payee
options.D: Four parties — Drawer, Drawee, Acceptor and Payee

answer_html:
Answer: (C) Three parties — Drawer, Drawee/Acceptor and Payee

Section 5: A BILL OF EXCHANGE has THREE PARTIES: (1) DRAWER — the maker who issues the order to pay; (2) DRAWEE/ACCEPTOR — the person directed to pay (becomes 'acceptor' after signing acceptance); and (3) PAYEE — the person to whom payment is to be made. A BoE contains an ORDER to pay (not a promise). It may be accepted conditionally.

question_html: Under Section 6 of the NI Act, a 'cheque' is defined as:

options.A: Any order to pay a specific sum of money on demand to a named person
options.B: A bill of exchange drawn on a SPECIFIED BANKER and NOT expressed to be payable otherwise than ON DEMAND — includes electronic image of truncated cheque and cheque in electronic form
options.C: A promissory note issued by a bank to its customer
options.D: A negotiable instrument requiring acceptance before payment

answer_html:
Answer: (B) A bill of exchange drawn on a SPECIFIED BANKER and NOT expressed to be payable otherwise than ON DEMAND — includes electronic image of truncated cheque and cheque in electronic form

Section 6: A CHEQUE = a BILL OF EXCHANGE drawn on a SPECIFIED BANKER and NOT expressed to be payable otherwise than ON DEMAND — includes the ELECTRONIC IMAGE OF A TRUNCATED CHEQUE and a CHEQUE IN ELECTRONIC FORM. Three parties: DRAWER (account holder), DRAWEE (always the BANK — specified banker), and PAYEE. Cheques do NOT require acceptance; no grace days; can be crossed; criminal liability for dishonour (Sec. 138). Amendment Act 2015 (w.e.f. 26.12.2015) added electronic cheque provisions.

question_html: A 'truncated cheque' under Section 6 is defined as:

options.A: A cheque that has been physically cut or torn by the bank
options.B: A cheque that is not payable on demand
options.C: A cheque which is truncated during the course of a clearing cycle by the clearing house or bank — immediately on generation of an electronic image for transmission — substituting the further physical movement of the cheque
options.D: A post-dated cheque presented before the due date

answer_html:
Answer: (A) A cheque that has been physically cut or torn by the bank

Section 6 (Amendment Act 2015, w.e.f. 26.12.2015): A TRUNCATED CHEQUE = a cheque which is TRUNCATED DURING THE COURSE OF A CLEARING CYCLE, either by the CLEARING HOUSE or by the BANK (paying or receiving), immediately on GENERATION OF AN ELECTRONIC IMAGE FOR TRANSMISSION, substituting the further PHYSICAL MOVEMENT of the cheque in writing. A 'clearing house' = managed by the RBI or recognized by RBI. A 'cheque in electronic form' = drawn using computer resource, signed with DIGITAL SIGNATURE (with/without biometric signature).

question_html: Which of the following is NOT an essential feature of a negotiable instrument?

options.A: It must be in writing and signed by the maker or drawer
options.B: The promise or order must be unconditional
options.C: It must be registered with the Sub-Registrar
options.D: It must call for payment of a certain sum in money only

answer_html:
Answer: (C) It must be registered with the Sub-Registrar

ESSENTIAL FEATURES of a Negotiable Instrument: (1) Must be IN WRITING; (2) Signed by maker/drawer; (3) Promise or ORDER to pay; (4) Promise/order must be UNCONDITIONAL; (5) Payment in MONEY AND MONEY ONLY; (6) CERTAIN SUM payable; (7) Property passes by MERE DELIVERY (bearer) or ENDORSEMENT AND DELIVERY (order); (8) CONSIDERATION is presumed. REGISTRATION is NOT required for negotiable instruments — this is a feature of immovable property transactions.

question_html: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a PROMISSORY NOTE from a BILL OF EXCHANGE?

options.A: A BoE contains a promise to pay; a promissory note contains an order to pay
options.B: A promissory note contains an UNCONDITIONAL PROMISE to pay and the maker has primary/absolute liability; a BoE contains an UNCONDITIONAL ORDER and the drawee's liability is secondary and conditional (until acceptance)
options.C: A promissory note has three parties; a BoE has two parties
options.D: A BoE cannot be crossed; a promissory note can be crossed

answer_html:
Answer: (B) A promissory note contains an UNCONDITIONAL PROMISE to pay and the maker has primary/absolute liability; a BoE contains an UNCONDITIONAL ORDER and the drawee's liability is secondary and conditional (until acceptance)

PROMISSORY NOTE vs BILL OF EXCHANGE: (1) PN = PROMISE to pay [Sec.4]; BoE = ORDER to pay [Sec.5]; (2) PN has TWO parties (Maker + Payee); BoE has THREE parties (Drawer + Drawee/Acceptor + Payee); (3) PN: No conditions; BoE: MAY BE ACCEPTED CONDITIONALLY; (4) PN: Maker's liability is PRIMARY AND ABSOLUTE; BoE: Drawee's liability is SECONDARY AND CONDITIONAL; (5) PN: Cannot be self-drawn; (6) PN: Stamp required; (7) PN: No crossing; (8) PN: Limitation 3 years; Cheque: 6 months.
topic_text: Promissory Note vs Bill of Exchange: Key Distinctions

question_html: Which of the following correctly states the distinction between a BILL OF EXCHANGE and a CHEQUE regarding grace days and acceptance?

options.A: Both require acceptance and neither has any grace days
options.B: Both have 3 days of grace and both require formal acceptance
options.C: A BoE generally has THREE DAYS OF GRACE for payment (not on demand BoEs); a CHEQUE requires NO GRACE DAYS and NO ACCEPTANCE; the drawee of a BoE may be anyone but in a cheque the drawee is ALWAYS A BANK
options.D: A cheque has 3 days of grace while a BoE has no grace days

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Both require acceptance and neither has any grace days

BILL OF EXCHANGE vs CHEQUE: (1) BoE: GENERALLY THREE DAYS OF GRACE (not for demand BoEs); Cheque: NO GRACE DAYS — immediate payment; (2) BoE: REQUIRES ACCEPTANCE; Cheque: NO ACCEPTANCE required; (3) BoE: Drawee can be ANY PERSON; Cheque: Drawee is ALWAYS A BANKER; (4) BoE: Civil liability on dishonour; Cheque: CRIMINAL LIABILITY under Sec. 138; (5) BoE: Cannot be crossed; Cheque: Can be CROSSED; (6) BoE: No statutory protection to paying banker; Cheque: Sec. 85 protection to banker.
topic_text: Bill of Exchange vs Cheque: Grace Days

question_html: Under Section 10, 'payment in due course' means payment made:

options.A: On the date specified in the instrument without any delay
options.B: By any person in possession of the instrument before maturity
options.C: In accordance with the apparent tenor of the instrument — in GOOD FAITH and WITHOUT NEGLIGENCE — to any person in possession thereof — under circumstances which do not afford a REASONABLE GROUND FOR BELIEVING that he is not entitled to receive payment
options.D: Only to the original payee named in the instrument

answer_html:
Answer: (C) In accordance with the apparent tenor of the instrument — in GOOD FAITH and WITHOUT NEGLIGENCE — to any person in possession thereof — under circumstances which do not afford a REASONABLE GROUND FOR BELIEVING that he is not entitled to receive payment

Section 10: PAYMENT IN DUE COURSE = payment (a) in accordance with the APPARENT TENOR of the instrument; (b) in GOOD FAITH AND WITHOUT NEGLIGENCE; (c) to any person IN POSSESSION thereof; (d) under circumstances which do NOT AFFORD A REASONABLE GROUND FOR BELIEVING that he is NOT ENTITLED TO RECEIVE PAYMENT. A banker's duty in paying a cheque is DISCHARGED BY PAYMENT IN DUE COURSE. Section 80: When no interest rate is specified in the instrument, interest is calculated at 18% per annum from the date of due to realisation. PARTIES, HOLDER & HOLDER IN DUE COURSE — SECTIONS 7–9, 26–44

question_html: Under Section 8, who is defined as the 'holder' of a negotiable instrument?

options.A: Any person physically possessing the instrument
options.B: Any person ENTITLED IN HIS OWN NAME to possession thereof and to RECEIVE OR RECOVER the amount due thereon from parties thereto — where the note/bill/cheque is lost or destroyed, the holder is the person so entitled AT THE TIME OF LOSS OR DESTRUCTION
options.C: Only the original payee named in the instrument
options.D: Only a person who has paid consideration for the instrument

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Any person ENTITLED IN HIS OWN NAME to possession thereof and to RECEIVE OR RECOVER the amount due thereon from parties thereto — where the note/bill/cheque is lost or destroyed, the holder is the person so entitled AT THE TIME OF LOSS OR DESTRUCTION

Section 8: HOLDER = any person ENTITLED IN HIS OWN NAME to: (a) POSSESSION of the promissory note, BoE or cheque; AND (b) RECEIVE OR RECOVER THE AMOUNT DUE thereon from parties. Case: Anjaniaih v. Nagappa (AIR 1967 AP 61) — the FINDER OF A LOST INSTRUMENT payable to bearer or a THIEF is NOT a holder (no right to recover). A person PROHIBITED BY COURT ORDER from receiving payment is also NOT a holder. Where the instrument is LOST OR DESTROYED, the holder is the person entitled AT THE TIME OF LOSS.

question_html: Under Section 9, a 'holder in due course' (HDC) is a person who became the possessor of a negotiable instrument — if payable to bearer — or the payee or endorsee — if payable to order — and satisfies which conditions?

options.A: For consideration; before the amount became payable; and WITHOUT SUFFICIENT CAUSE TO BELIEVE any defect existed in the title of the person from whom he derived title
options.B: For consideration and after the amount became payable
options.C: Without consideration but in good faith before maturity
options.D: For consideration only — good faith and timing are not required

answer_html:
Answer: (A) For consideration; before the amount became payable; and WITHOUT SUFFICIENT CAUSE TO BELIEVE any defect existed in the title of the person from whom he derived title

Section 9: HOLDER IN DUE COURSE must satisfy THREE CONDITIONS: (1) For CONSIDERATION — became possessor for value; (2) BEFORE THE AMOUNT BECAME PAYABLE (i.e., before maturity); and (3) WITHOUT HAVING SUFFICIENT CAUSE TO BELIEVE that ANY DEFECT EXISTED IN THE TITLE of the person from whom he derived title. (Braja Kishore Dikshit v. Purna Chandra Panda, AIR 1957). A HDC gets a BETTER TITLE than the transferor — unlike ordinary holder whose title is subject to transferor's title.

question_html: Which of the following CORRECTLY distinguishes a 'holder' from a 'holder in due course'?

options.A: Both get identical rights — there is no practical difference
options.B: A holder can receive the instrument gratuitously; a holder in due course always receives for consideration
options.C: A holder always gets a better title than the transferor; a holder in due course does not necessarily get a better title
options.D: Only a holder can sue on the instrument; a holder in due course cannot

answer_html:
Answer: (C) A holder always gets a better title than the transferor; a holder in due course does not necessarily get a better title

HOLDER vs HOLDER IN DUE COURSE: (1) Holder may receive WITHOUT CONSIDERATION; HDC always receives FOR CONSIDERATION; (2) Holder's title is SUBJECT TO DEFECTS of transferor; HDC gets a BETTER TITLE than transferor (free from defects); (3) Holder gets the instrument ANY TIME; HDC must receive BEFORE MATURITY; (4) Holder does not get certain PRIVILEGES available to HDC; (5) Section 53: A holder deriving title FROM a HDC also gets the RIGHTS of a HDC. Section 36: Every prior party is liable to a HDC until the instrument is duly satisfied.
topic_text: Holder vs Holder in Due Course: Key Distinctions

question_html: Under Section 26, a MINOR may deal with negotiable instruments in which of the following ways?

options.A: A minor cannot deal with negotiable instruments in any manner
options.B: A minor may DRAW, INDORSE, DELIVER AND NEGOTIATE such instruments so as to BIND ALL PARTIES EXCEPT HIMSELF — the minor incurs no personal liability
options.C: A minor can make, draw, accept and negotiate instruments with full personal liability
options.D: A minor can only accept a bill of exchange — no other dealings are permitted

answer_html:
Answer: (B) A minor may DRAW, INDORSE, DELIVER AND NEGOTIATE such instruments so as to BIND ALL PARTIES EXCEPT HIMSELF — the minor incurs no personal liability

Section 26: Every person capable of contracting may bind himself and be bound by making/drawing/accepting/indorsing/delivering/negotiating a negotiable instrument. A MINOR MAY DRAW, INDORSE, DELIVER AND NEGOTIATE such instruments so as to BIND ALL PARTIES EXCEPT HIMSELF. The minor's signature does not impose any personal liability on the minor — but all other parties who signed the instrument remain liable. Case: Sulochana v. Panidyan Bank (AIR 1975 Mad 70): when a minor and another execute a promissory note, the other co-executor remains fully liable.

question_html: Under Section 28, if an AGENT signs his name to a promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque WITHOUT INDICATING that he signs as an agent or that he does not intend personal responsibility, the agent is:

options.A: Personally liable on the instrument — EXCEPT to those who induced him to sign upon the belief that the principal only would be held liable
options.B: Not personally liable — only the principal is liable
options.C: Jointly liable with the principal on the instrument
options.D: Not liable unless the amount exceeds Rs. 5,000

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Personally liable on the instrument — EXCEPT to those who induced him to sign upon the belief that the principal only would be held liable

Section 28: An AGENT who signs his name to a negotiable instrument WITHOUT INDICATING that he signs as agent or that he DOES NOT INTEND PERSONAL RESPONSIBILITY, is PERSONALLY LIABLE on the instrument — EXCEPT to those who INDUCED HIM TO SIGN upon the belief that the PRINCIPAL ONLY would be held liable. This is an exception to the general agency law principle where an undisclosed principal can be sued. The agent must clearly indicate his agency status to avoid personal liability.

question_html: Under Section 31, the DRAWEE of a cheque (i.e., the bank) having SUFFICIENT FUNDS of the drawer applicable to payment of such cheque must pay when duly required. In default of such payment, the bank must:

options.A: Compensate the PAYEE for any loss caused by such default
options.B: Return the cheque with the memo 'Refer to Drawer'
options.C: Compensate the DRAWER for any loss or damage caused by such default
options.D: Pay the cheque from its own funds

answer_html:
Answer: (C) Compensate the DRAWER for any loss or damage caused by such default

Section 31: The DRAWEE (BANK) having SUFFICIENT FUNDS of the drawer properly applicable to the payment of a cheque MUST PAY the cheque when duly required to do so. In DEFAULT OF SUCH PAYMENT, the bank must COMPENSATE THE DRAWER for any LOSS OR DAMAGE caused by such default. Note: The liability under Sec. 31 is to the DRAWER — not to the payee. This is the bank's contractual obligation to its customer (the drawer/account holder).
topic_text: Section 31 — Liability of Drawee of Cheque

question_html: Under Section 35, an indorser who indorses and delivers a negotiable instrument BEFORE MATURITY (without expressly excluding or making conditional his liability) is:

options.A: Not liable to any subsequent holder
options.B: Bound to every SUBSEQUENT HOLDER — in case of dishonour by drawee, acceptor or maker — to COMPENSATE SUCH HOLDER FOR ANY LOSS OR DAMAGE caused by dishonour — PROVIDED DUE NOTICE OF DISHONOUR has been given to or received by the indorser
options.C: Liable only to the immediate endorsee — not to subsequent holders
options.D: Liable only if he expressly guaranteed payment

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Bound to every SUBSEQUENT HOLDER — in case of dishonour by drawee, acceptor or maker — to COMPENSATE SUCH HOLDER FOR ANY LOSS OR DAMAGE caused by dishonour — PROVIDED DUE NOTICE OF DISHONOUR has been given to or received by the indorser

Section 35: An INDORSER who indorses and delivers a negotiable instrument BEFORE MATURITY (without expressly excluding or making his liability conditional) is BOUND to EVERY SUBSEQUENT HOLDER to COMPENSATE SUCH HOLDER for ANY LOSS OR DAMAGE by DISHONOUR — provided DUE NOTICE OF DISHONOUR has been given. Section 36: EVERY PRIOR PARTY to a negotiable instrument is liable to a HOLDER IN DUE COURSE until the instrument is DULY SATISFIED. Section 37: Maker of PN or Cheque, drawer of BoE until acceptance, and acceptor are PRINCIPAL DEBTORS; other parties are SURETIES. CROSSING, ENDORSEMENT & MATERIAL ALTERATION — SECTIONS 15–16, 123–131

question_html: Under Section 123, a cheque is said to be CROSSED GENERALLY when it bears across its face:

options.A: The name of a specific bank between two parallel transverse lines
options.B: The signature of the payee
options.C: The words 'and company' or any abbreviation between TWO PARALLEL TRANSVERSE LINES, OR two parallel transverse lines simply (with or without the words 'not negotiable')
options.D: The words 'account payee only' without any parallel lines

answer_html:
Answer: (A) The name of a specific bank between two parallel transverse lines

Section 123: GENERAL CROSSING = cheque bears across its face: (a) the words 'AND COMPANY' or ANY ABBREVIATION thereof, BETWEEN TWO PARALLEL TRANSVERSE LINES; or (b) TWO PARALLEL TRANSVERSE LINES SIMPLY — either with or without the words 'NOT NEGOTIABLE'. The effect of general crossing: payment can only be made THROUGH A BANKER (not over the counter). Section 124: SPECIAL CROSSING = name of a SPECIFIC BANKER added (with/without 'not negotiable'). Payment then only through that SPECIFIC BANKER.

question_html: Under Section 125, which of the following powers regarding crossing of a cheque is CORRECT?

options.A: Only the drawer can cross a cheque — no one else has this power
options.B: Only the bank can cross or un-cross a cheque
options.C: A holder may cross an uncrossed cheque generally or specially; a holder may cross a generally-crossed cheque specially; any holder may add 'not negotiable'; a specially-crossed banker may re-cross to another banker as agent for collection
options.D: Once crossed, a cheque cannot be crossed to a different bank

answer_html:
Answer: (C) A holder may cross an uncrossed cheque generally or specially; a holder may cross a generally-crossed cheque specially; any holder may add 'not negotiable'; a specially-crossed banker may re-cross to another banker as agent for collection

Section 125: (i) Where a cheque is NOT CROSSED — the HOLDER may cross it GENERALLY or SPECIALLY; (ii) Where CROSSED GENERALLY — the holder may cross it SPECIALLY; (iii) Where CROSSED GENERALLY OR SPECIALLY — the holder may add 'NOT NEGOTIABLE'; (iv) Where CROSSED SPECIALLY — the banker to whom it is crossed may AGAIN CROSS SPECIALLY to another banker as HIS AGENT FOR COLLECTION. This layering of crossing provides increasing security for the payee.
topic_text: Section 125 — Who May Cross a Cheque

question_html: Under Section 130, a person taking a cheque crossed with the words 'NOT NEGOTIABLE' shall:

options.A: Be able to freely transfer the cheque as with any other negotiable instrument
options.B: NOT HAVE AND SHALL NOT BE CAPABLE OF GIVING a BETTER TITLE to the cheque than which the person from whom he took it had
options.C: Be entitled to receive double the amount as compensation if the cheque bounces
options.D: Be deemed the holder in due course of the instrument

answer_html:
Answer: (B) NOT HAVE AND SHALL NOT BE CAPABLE OF GIVING a BETTER TITLE to the cheque than which the person from whom he took it had

Section 130: A person taking a cheque crossed generally or specially bearing 'NOT NEGOTIABLE' shall NOT HAVE, AND SHALL NOT BE CAPABLE OF GIVING, A BETTER TITLE TO THE CHEQUE than THAT WHICH THE PERSON FROM WHOM HE TOOK IT HAD. Effect: the cheque LOSES ITS NEGOTIABILITY — the transferee acquires only the title of the transferor; a bona fide purchaser for value does not get a better title. Example: if Y's title is defective, Z who takes from Y with 'not negotiable' crossing also gets defective title.

question_html: Under Section 131, a banker who has IN GOOD FAITH AND WITHOUT NEGLIGENCE received payment for a customer of a cheque crossed generally or specially to himself — in case the title of the cheque proves defective — incurs:

options.A: No liability to the true owner of the cheque by reason only of having received such payment
options.B: Full liability to the true owner for the entire amount received
options.C: Joint liability with the customer for whom payment was collected
options.D: Liability only if he had knowledge of the defective title

answer_html:
Answer: (A) No liability to the true owner of the cheque by reason only of having received such payment

Section 131: A BANKER who has IN GOOD FAITH AND WITHOUT NEGLIGENCE received payment for a customer of a crossed cheque shall NOT, IN CASE THE TITLE OF THE CHEQUE PROVES DEFECTIVE, INCUR ANY LIABILITY TO THE TRUE OWNER by reason only of having received such payment. The banker is also PROTECTED even if he credits the customer's account BEFORE receiving actual payment. For truncated cheques, the receiving bank must VERIFY THE PRIMA FACIE GENUINENESS of the image and check for any apparent fraud, forgery or tampering.

question_html: Under Section 15, endorsement (indorsement) of a negotiable instrument means:

options.A: The signature of the maker on the face of the instrument
options.B: The acceptance of the bill of exchange by the drawee
options.C: When the maker or holder of a negotiable instrument signs the same — OTHER THAN AS MAKER — for the purpose of NEGOTIATION on the back or face thereof, or on a slip of paper annexed thereto (called allonge)
options.D: The certification by a notary public of the instrument

answer_html:
Answer: (C) When the maker or holder of a negotiable instrument signs the same — OTHER THAN AS MAKER — for the purpose of NEGOTIATION on the back or face thereof, or on a slip of paper annexed thereto (called allonge)

Section 15: ENDORSEMENT = when the MAKER OR HOLDER of a negotiable instrument signs the same — OTHER THAN AS MAKER — for the purpose of NEGOTIATION on the BACK OR FACE thereof, or on a SLIP OF PAPER ANNEXED thereto (ALLONGE). The person signing = INDORSER; the person in whose favour endorsed = ENDORSEE. Key: the first endorsement of an instrument can only be made by the PAYEE; subsequent endorsements can be made by ANY HOLDER. Endorsement is COMPLETE when the instrument is DELIVERED to the endorsee.

question_html: Under Section 16, if the endorser signs his name ONLY without adding a direction to pay to a specific person, the endorsement is called:

options.A: Full endorsement — naming the endorsee
options.B: Restrictive endorsement — limiting further negotiation
options.C: BLANK (general) endorsement — payable to the bearer; the holder of a blank-endorsed instrument may WITHOUT SIGNING HIS OWN NAME convert it to a FULL endorsement by writing a direction above the endorser's signature
options.D: Conditional endorsement — subject to a specified event

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Restrictive endorsement — limiting further negotiation

Section 16(1): If the endorser SIGNS HIS NAME ONLY — BLANK (IN BLANK) endorsement — the instrument becomes PAYABLE TO BEARER. Section 49: Holder of a blank-endorsed instrument may, WITHOUT SIGNING HIS OWN NAME, by writing above the endorser's signature a direction to pay to another person, CONVERT THE BLANK ENDORSEMENT INTO A FULL ENDORSEMENT — the holder does NOT thereby incur the responsibility of an endorser. FULL endorsement adds a specific endorsee. RESTRICTIVE endorsement restricts further negotiation (e.g., 'Pay A only'). CONDITIONAL endorsement makes liability depend on a specified event.

question_html: Under Section 52, when an endorser adds the words 'WITHOUT RECOURSE' or 'SANS RECOURSE' to his endorsement, the effect is:

options.A: The endorser is still fully liable on dishonour of the instrument
options.B: The endorsement is void — such conditions cannot be added
options.C: He EXCLUDES HIS OWN LIABILITY — subsequent holders cannot look to him for payment if the instrument is dishonoured; but where he so excludes his liability and afterwards becomes the holder, all INTERMEDIATE ENDORSERS are liable to him
options.D: The instrument ceases to be negotiable after such endorsement

answer_html:
Answer: (A) The endorser is still fully liable on dishonour of the instrument

Section 52: SANS RECOURSE / WITHOUT RECOURSE ENDORSEMENT: The endorser EXCLUDES HIS OWN LIABILITY — on dishonour, subsequent holders CANNOT LOOK TO HIM FOR PAYMENT. He can add: 'Pay A or order — without recourse to me' or 'Sans recourse' or 'at A's own risk'. SPECIAL RULE: where the endorser EXCLUDES HIS LIABILITY and AFTERWARDS BECOMES THE HOLDER of the instrument, ALL INTERMEDIATE ENDORSERS are liable to him. SANS FRAIS endorsement = endorser does not want any EXPENSE INCURRED on his account.

question_html: A 'material alteration' of a negotiable instrument renders the instrument:

options.A: Voidable at the option of the holder in due course
options.B: Valid if the alteration benefits the party liable on it
options.C: VOID as against anyone who was a party thereto at the time of making the alteration and did NOT CONSENT — unless made to carry out the COMMON INTENTION of the original parties; and if made by an endorsee, DISCHARGES THE ENDORSER from all liability
options.D: Only voidable if the alteration changes the amount payable

answer_html:
Answer: (C) VOID as against anyone who was a party thereto at the time of making the alteration and did NOT CONSENT — unless made to carry out the COMMON INTENTION of the original parties; and if made by an endorsee, DISCHARGES THE ENDORSER from all liability

MATERIAL ALTERATION renders the instrument VOID as against: (a) any party thereto AT THE TIME OF ALTERATION; (b) who did NOT CONSENT to it. EXCEPTION: alteration made to carry out the COMMON INTENTION of original parties. Case: Lokaram Sethiya v. Ivon E John (1977 SC): a material alteration is one which VARIES RIGHTS, LIABILITIES OR LEGAL POSITION of parties. Material alterations include: changing bearer to order cheque, altering amount, date of payment, sum payable, time of payment, rate of interest, place of payment, or adding a new party. NON-MATERIAL alterations include: conversion of general crossing to special crossing, completion of inchoate instrument, correcting mistakes, adding a blank endorsement to full endorsement. ACCEPTANCE, NEGOTIATION & SPECIAL INSTRUMENTS — SECTIONS 14, 46–60

question_html: Under Section 14, when is a promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque said to be 'NEGOTIATED'?

options.A: When it is sold by the holder for consideration
options.B: When it is transferred to any person so as to CONSTITUTE THAT PERSON THE HOLDER thereof
options.C: When it is assigned by a written document to another person
options.D: When it is surrendered to the drawee for payment

answer_html:
Answer: (B) When it is transferred to any person so as to CONSTITUTE THAT PERSON THE HOLDER thereof

Section 14: NEGOTIATION = when a promissory note, BoE or cheque is TRANSFERRED TO ANY PERSON so as to CONSTITUTE THAT PERSON THE HOLDER THEREOF. TWO TYPES: (1) NEGOTIATION BY DELIVERY [Sec.47] — instrument payable to BEARER; (2) NEGOTIATION BY ENDORSEMENT AND DELIVERY [Sec.48] — instrument payable to ORDER. Section 60: A negotiable instrument may be negotiated (except by maker, drawee or acceptor after maturity) UNTIL PAYMENT OR SATISFACTION at or after maturity — but NOT AFTER such payment.

question_html: Under the NI Act, what is a 'QUALIFIED ACCEPTANCE' of a bill of exchange and what is its effect?

options.A: Acceptance without any qualification — the holder has no option to treat it as dishonoured
options.B: When the drawee accepts the bill WITHOUT QUALIFICATION — an unqualified acceptance
options.C: An acceptance subject to some QUALIFICATION — e.g., partial amount, conditional on an event, at a specified place only, or at a different time — the holder may treat the bill as DISHONOURED BY NON-ACCEPTANCE and all prior parties whose consent is not obtained are DISCHARGED as against the holder
options.D: Acceptance by a person other than the drawee

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Acceptance without any qualification — the holder has no option to treat it as dishonoured

QUALIFIED ACCEPTANCE [Section 86]: Acceptance subject to QUALIFICATION regarding: (a) event (accepted payable when in funds); (b) PART ONLY of sum (accepted for Rs. 900 against Rs. 1,000); (c) SPECIFIC PLACE of choice; (d) DIFFERENT TIME; (e) not signed by ALL drawees (non-partners). EFFECT: (a) Holder may TREAT THE BILL AS DISHONOURED and sue drawer and prior endorsers; (b) if the holder ACCEPTS the qualified acceptance, ALL PRIOR PARTIES WHOSE CONSENT IS NOT OBTAINED are DISCHARGED as against the holder and those deriving title from him.

question_html: Under Section 22, for a promissory note or bill of exchange NOT payable on demand, at sight, or on presentment, the MATURITY DATE is:

options.A: The exact date expressed in the instrument — no additional days are added
options.B: Two days after the date expressed in the instrument
options.C: The THIRD DAY on which it is expressed to be payable — i.e., THREE DAYS OF GRACE are added
options.D: Seven days after the date expressed in the instrument

answer_html:
Answer: (C) The THIRD DAY on which it is expressed to be payable — i.e., THREE DAYS OF GRACE are added

Section 22: The MATURITY of a promissory note or BoE (not payable on demand, at sight, or on presentment) = the THIRD DAY on which it is EXPRESSED TO BE PAYABLE. So THREE DAYS OF GRACE are added. Example: if a BoE is drawn payable 30 days after date, maturity = 33rd day. CHEQUES are payable on DEMAND — no days of grace. Section 23: When calculating maturity by months — the period terminates on the day of the month corresponding to the date the instrument was drawn; if that month has no such day, the period ends on the LAST DAY of that month.

question_html: Under Section 118, in the absence of proof to the contrary, which of the following presumptions shall be made as to a negotiable instrument?

options.A: No presumptions — everything must be specifically proved
options.B: The instrument was made for consideration; made on the stated date; accepted within reasonable time before maturity; transferred before maturity; endorsements in stated order; duly stamped; the holder is a HOLDER IN DUE COURSE
options.C: Only that consideration was paid — no other presumptions
options.D: Only that the instrument was made on the stated date and duly stamped

answer_html:
Answer: (B) The instrument was made for consideration; made on the stated date; accepted within reasonable time before maturity; transferred before maturity; endorsements in stated order; duly stamped; the holder is a HOLDER IN DUE COURSE

Section 118 STATUTORY PRESUMPTIONS (until contrary proved): (1) CONSIDERATION — made/drawn for consideration; (2) DATE — made/drawn on stated date; (3) ACCEPTANCE TIME — accepted within reasonable time after date and before maturity; (4) TRANSFER — made before maturity; (5) ORDER OF ENDORSEMENTS — in the order they appear; (6) STAMP — duly stamped; (7) HOLDER IS A HDC. Section 119: PRESUMPTION ON PROOF OF PROTEST — in a suit on a dishonoured instrument, on proof of protest, the court presumes the FACT OF DISHONOUR unless disproved.

question_html: Under Section 56, is it valid to endorse a negotiable instrument for PART of the amount due on it?

options.A: A partial endorsement is always valid if the endorsee consents to it
options.B: No partial endorsement is valid for the purpose of NEGOTIATION — UNLESS a part has been PAID AND NOTED ON THE INSTRUMENT, in which case the endorsement of the BALANCE is valid
options.C: Partial endorsement is valid only for cheques — not for bills or promissory notes
options.D: A partial endorsement is valid if witnessed by two persons

answer_html:
Answer: (A) A partial endorsement is always valid if the endorsee consents to it

Section 56: No writing on a negotiable instrument is VALID FOR THE PURPOSE OF NEGOTIATION if it purports to transfer only a PART OF THE AMOUNT appearing to be due. EXCEPTION: Where the amount has been PARTLY PAID, a note to that effect may be endorsed on the instrument, and the instrument may then be NEGOTIATED FOR THE BALANCE. The logic is that an instrument represents a single obligation; splitting it would complicate the legal position of multiple parties.

question_html: When a person signs and delivers to another a BLANK or INCOMPLETE paper stamped as a negotiable instrument, what authority does this confer on the holder?

options.A: No authority — a blank instrument creates no obligation
options.B: Authority only up to Rs. 5,000 regardless of stamp value
options.C: PRIMA FACIE AUTHORITY to MAKE OR COMPLETE a negotiable instrument for any amount NOT EXCEEDING the amount covered by the stamp — the signing person is liable on such instrument TO ANY HOLDER IN DUE COURSE for such amount; but no person other than a HDC can recover MORE than the AMOUNT INTENDED by the signatory
options.D: Authority to complete only if both parties sign the instrument later

answer_html:
Answer: (C) PRIMA FACIE AUTHORITY to MAKE OR COMPLETE a negotiable instrument for any amount NOT EXCEEDING the amount covered by the stamp — the signing person is liable on such instrument TO ANY HOLDER IN DUE COURSE for such amount; but no person other than a HDC can recover MORE than the AMOUNT INTENDED by the signatory

INCHOATE STAMPED INSTRUMENT: Where a person signs and delivers a STAMPED PAPER (wholly blank or incomplete), he gives PRIMA FACIE AUTHORITY to the holder to MAKE OR COMPLETE a negotiable instrument for any amount not exceeding the AMOUNT COVERED BY THE STAMP. The signing person is LIABLE to a HOLDER IN DUE COURSE for such amount. However, NO PERSON OTHER THAN A HDC shall recover MORE than the AMOUNT INTENDED by the signatory. Case: Unsolved case — 'C' as HDC can recover Rs. 2,000 (the stamp-covered amount), not Rs. 500 as originally authorised.

question_html: Under Section 57, if a negotiable instrument has been LOST OR OBTAINED BY FRAUD/OFFENCE from its maker, acceptor or holder, who can claim payment from the maker/acceptor/holder?

options.A: Any person in possession of the instrument
options.B: Only a HOLDER IN DUE COURSE (or someone deriving title through a HDC) — any possessor or endorsee who claims through the person who found or fraudulently obtained the instrument is NOT entitled to receive payment
options.C: The finder of the instrument, as the current possessor
options.D: Any person who gave consideration for the instrument

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Only a HOLDER IN DUE COURSE (or someone deriving title through a HDC) — any possessor or endorsee who claims through the person who found or fraudulently obtained the instrument is NOT entitled to receive payment

Section 57: When a negotiable instrument has been LOST or obtained by OFFENCE, FRAUD or UNLAWFUL CONSIDERATION, no possessor or endorsee who CLAIMS THROUGH THE PERSON who found or so obtained it is entitled to receive the amount — UNLESS SUCH POSSESSOR OR ENDORSEE IS, OR SOME PERSON THROUGH WHOM HE CLAIMS WAS, A HOLDER IN DUE COURSE. The HDC protection is critical — it cuts through even fraud or unlawful acquisition by predecessors in title.
topic_text: Section 57 — Instrument Obtained by Unlawful Means

question_html: Which of the following correctly distinguishes NEGOTIATION from ASSIGNMENT of a negotiable instrument?

options.A: Negotiation requires written notice to the debtor; assignment does not
options.B: In negotiation, consideration is PRESUMED; a HDC takes FREE FROM DEFECTS; notice of transfer is NOT necessary; transferee can sue in his OWN NAME — in assignment, CONSIDERATION MUST BE PROVED; assignee's title is SUBJECT TO EQUITIES; NOTICE MUST BE GIVEN to debtor; assignment effected by WRITING only
options.C: Both negotiation and assignment give identical rights to the transferee
options.D: Assignment gives a better title than negotiation

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Negotiation requires written notice to the debtor; assignment does not

NEGOTIATION vs ASSIGNMENT: NEGOTIATION: (1) Consideration PRESUMED; (2) HDC takes FREE FROM DEFECTS; (3) Notice of transfer NOT necessary; (4) Transferee can SUE IN OWN NAME; (5) Effected by DELIVERY (bearer) or ENDORSEMENT+DELIVERY (order); (6) Many presumptions in favour of HDC. ASSIGNMENT: (1) Consideration must be PROVED; (2) Assignee's title SUBJECT TO EQUITIES; (3) NOTICE of assignment must be given; (4) Assignee CANNOT sue in own name; (5) Effected by WRITING only; (6) No presumptions in favour of assignee. Under Transfer of Property Act Sec. 130 — assignment as chose in action. DISHONOUR, NOTICE, NOTING, PROTEST & SECTION 138 — SECTIONS 91–147

question_html: Under Sections 91 and 92, a negotiable instrument may be dishonoured in which two ways?

options.A: By forfeiture and by lapse of time
options.B: By non-payment and by cancellation
options.C: By NON-ACCEPTANCE [Section 91] — when the drawee makes default in acceptance upon being duly required, or acceptance is qualified or drawee is incompetent; AND by NON-PAYMENT [Section 92] — when the maker, acceptor or drawee makes default in payment upon being duly required
options.D: By endorsement and by novation

answer_html:
Answer: (C) By NON-ACCEPTANCE [Section 91] — when the drawee makes default in acceptance upon being duly required, or acceptance is qualified or drawee is incompetent; AND by NON-PAYMENT [Section 92] — when the maker, acceptor or drawee makes default in payment upon being duly required

Section 91: DISHONOUR BY NON-ACCEPTANCE — bill is dishonoured when the DRAWEE (or one of several non-partner drawees) MAKES DEFAULT IN ACCEPTANCE, or where presentment is excused and bill is not accepted; OR when drawee is INCOMPETENT TO CONTRACT; OR acceptance is QUALIFIED. Section 92: DISHONOUR BY NON-PAYMENT — when the MAKER OF NOTE, ACCEPTOR OF BILL, or DRAWEE OF CHEQUE makes DEFAULT IN PAYMENT upon being duly required to pay.

question_html: Under Section 94, the notice of dishonour may be given in which form?

options.A: Only in writing — oral notice is never valid
options.B: In WRITING OR ORAL — if in writing, it must be sent by POST and must inform the party either in express terms or by reasonable intendment that the instrument has been dishonoured and he will be held liable thereon
options.C: Only through a notary public — informal notice has no legal effect
options.D: Only at a court proceeding — informal notice is insufficient

answer_html:
Answer: (B) In WRITING OR ORAL — if in writing, it must be sent by POST and must inform the party either in express terms or by reasonable intendment that the instrument has been dishonoured and he will be held liable thereon

Section 93: When an instrument is DISHONOURED, the HOLDER MUST GIVE NOTICE that the instrument has been dishonoured. Section 94: Notice may be IN WRITING OR ORAL. If in WRITTEN FORM, must be SENT BY POST. It must inform the party — in express terms or by REASONABLE INTENDMENT — that the instrument has been dishonoured and he WILL BE HELD LIABLE thereon. It must be given within a REASONABLE TIME after dishonour, at the PLACE OF BUSINESS OR RESIDENCE of the party. For BoE notice of dishonour is STRICTLY NECESSARY to charge the drawer; for a cheque, the banker returning the cheque with memo 'Refer to Drawer' is sufficient notice.

question_html: Under Section 98, in which of the following situations is notice of dishonour NOT necessary?

options.A: When it is dispensed with by the party entitled thereto; the drawer has countermanded payment; the party charged cannot suffer damage for want of notice; the party cannot be found; the party promises unconditionally to pay after knowing the facts; the promissory note is not negotiable; or the acceptor is also the drawer
options.B: Notice is always mandatory — there are no exceptions
options.C: Only when the cheque is crossed 'not negotiable'
options.D: Only when the instrument has been materially altered

answer_html:
Answer: (A) When it is dispensed with by the party entitled thereto; the drawer has countermanded payment; the party charged cannot suffer damage for want of notice; the party cannot be found; the party promises unconditionally to pay after knowing the facts; the promissory note is not negotiable; or the acceptor is also the drawer

Section 98: NOTICE OF DISHONOUR NOT NECESSARY when: (1) DISPENSED WITH by the party entitled to it; (2) DRAWER COUNTERMANDED PAYMENT; (3) The party charged CANNOT SUFFER DAMAGE for want of notice; (4) The party ENTITLED TO NOTICE CANNOT BE FOUND after due search or the party bound to give notice is UNABLE TO GIVE IT without his own fault; (5) To charge DRAWERS when the ACCEPTOR IS ALSO A DRAWER; (6) In case of a PROMISSORY NOTE WHICH IS NOT NEGOTIABLE; (7) When the party entitled to notice KNOWING THE FACTS, UNCONDITIONALLY PROMISES TO PAY.
topic_text: Section 98 — When Notice of Dishonour is NOT Necessary

question_html: Under Section 99, when an instrument is DISHONOURED, the holder may cause the dishonour to be NOTED by a notary public. What must the noting specify?

options.A: Only the date of dishonour and the reason
options.B: Only the notary's signature and the instrument details
options.C: The DATE OF DISHONOUR; the REASON assigned for such dishonour (or the reason the holder treats it as dishonoured if not expressly dishonoured); and the NOTARY'S CHARGES
options.D: A complete transcript of the instrument and the notary's certificate

answer_html:
Answer: (C) The DATE OF DISHONOUR; the REASON assigned for such dishonour (or the reason the holder treats it as dishonoured if not expressly dishonoured); and the NOTARY'S CHARGES

Section 99: NOTING = the holder may cause dishonour to be NOTED BY A NOTARY PUBLIC upon the instrument or upon a paper attached thereto or partly upon each. Must be made within a REASONABLE TIME after dishonour. Noting must specify: (1) DATE OF DISHONOUR; (2) REASON assigned for dishonour (or reason holder treats it as dishonoured); and (3) NOTARY'S CHARGES. Section 100: PROTEST = when the holder may cause such dishonour to be NOTED AND CERTIFIED by a notary public — such certificate = PROTEST. PROTEST FOR BETTER SECURITY: when the acceptor becomes insolvent or his credit has been publicly impeached before maturity.

question_html: For an offence under Section 138 to be constituted (penalty for dishonour of cheque), which of the following conditions must ALL be satisfied?

options.A: The cheque must be presented within 6 months and the payee must send notice within 15 days
options.B: The cheque must be drawn for any payment, presented within 3 months, and dishonoured for any reason
options.C: (1) Cheque drawn for DISCHARGE OF LEGALLY ENFORCEABLE DEBT or other liability; (2) Presented within 3 MONTHS (or period of validity, whichever earlier); (3) Returned UNPAID due to INSUFFICIENT FUNDS or exceeding overdraft arrangement; (4) Payee gives WRITTEN DEMAND NOTICE within 30 DAYS of receiving information of dishonour; (5) Drawer FAILS TO PAY within 15 DAYS of receipt of demand notice
options.D: The cheque must be presented within 6 months, notice given within 30 days, and payment not made within 30 days

answer_html:
Answer: (B) The cheque must be drawn for any payment, presented within 3 months, and dishonoured for any reason

Section 138 FIVE CONDITIONS for offence: (1) Cheque drawn for DISCHARGE IN WHOLE OR PART of any LEGALLY ENFORCEABLE DEBT or liability; (2) Presented to BANK WITHIN 3 MONTHS (effective 01.04.2012 — earlier 6 months) from date of drawing or within period of its VALIDITY, whichever earlier; (3) Returned by bank UNPAID due to INSUFFICIENT FUNDS or exceeding ARRANGED AMOUNT; (4) PAYEE GIVES WRITTEN DEMAND NOTICE TO DRAWER WITHIN 30 DAYS of receiving information from bank; (5) DRAWER FAILS TO PAY within 15 DAYS of receipt of notice. If all five conditions are met, drawer shall be punished.

question_html: Under Section 138, the punishment for dishonour of cheque for insufficiency of funds is:

options.A: Imprisonment up to 1 year or fine up to the cheque amount, or both
options.B: Only a fine — no imprisonment
options.C: Imprisonment up to 2 YEARS or fine up to TWICE THE AMOUNT OF THE CHEQUE, or both — without prejudice to any other provisions of the Act
options.D: Imprisonment up to 5 years and fine equal to the cheque amount

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Imprisonment up to 1 year or fine up to the cheque amount, or both

Section 138: Punishment = IMPRISONMENT for a term which may be EXTENDED TO 2 YEARS, OR FINE which may extend to TWICE THE AMOUNT OF THE CHEQUE, OR BOTH — without prejudice to any other provision of the Act. Section 140: It is NOT A DEFENCE that the drawer HAD NO REASON TO BELIEVE the cheque may be dishonoured when he issued it. Section 143A (2018 Amendment): Court may direct drawer to pay INTERIM COMPENSATION UP TO 20% of the cheque amount when he pleads 'not guilty'.

question_html: Under Section 139, when a cheque is received (of the nature referred to in Section 138), it is presumed unless the contrary is proved that the holder received the cheque:

options.A: For any lawful purpose including gifting
options.B: Only for the payment of an existing acknowledged debt
options.C: For the DISCHARGE, IN WHOLE OR IN PART, of any DEBT OR OTHER LIABILITY
options.D: Without consideration — the burden is on the holder to prove consideration

answer_html:
Answer: (C) For the DISCHARGE, IN WHOLE OR IN PART, of any DEBT OR OTHER LIABILITY

Section 139: It shall be PRESUMED, unless the CONTRARY IS PROVED, that the holder of a cheque under Section 138 received the cheque for the DISCHARGE, IN WHOLE OR IN PART, of any DEBT OR OTHER LIABILITY. This creates a REBUTTABLE PRESUMPTION in favour of the holder. Case: B. Mohan Krishna v. Union of India (AP HC): this presumption is NOT VIOLATIVE of Article 20(3) of the Constitution (protection against self-incrimination). The accused drawer must rebut this presumption.
topic_text: Section 139 — Presumption in Favour of Holder

question_html: Under Section 141, if a COMPANY commits an offence under Section 138 (dishonour of cheque), who is liable to be prosecuted?

options.A: Only the company as a legal entity — no individual officer is liable
options.B: The company AND every person who at the time of the offence was IN CHARGE OF AND RESPONSIBLE to the company for the conduct of business — UNLESS the person proves the offence was committed WITHOUT HIS KNOWLEDGE or he exercised DUE DILIGENCE to prevent it
options.C: Only the Managing Director and Chairman
options.D: Only the Finance Director as the cheque relates to financial matters

answer_html:
Answer: (B) The company AND every person who at the time of the offence was IN CHARGE OF AND RESPONSIBLE to the company for the conduct of business — UNLESS the person proves the offence was committed WITHOUT HIS KNOWLEDGE or he exercised DUE DILIGENCE to prevent it

Section 141(1): If the person committing an offence under the Act is a COMPANY — the COMPANY and EVERY PERSON who at the time of the offence was IN CHARGE OF AND RESPONSIBLE to the company for the conduct of business shall be deemed GUILTY OF THE OFFENCE and liable to punishment. EXCEPTION: A person is not liable if he proves the offence was committed WITHOUT HIS KNOWLEDGE or he exercised ALL DUE DILIGENCE to prevent it. A Director nominated by Central Govt./State Govt./Financial Corporation shall NOT be liable for prosecution. Section 141(2): Where offence is committed with CONSENT, CONNIVANCE OR NEGLECT of a director/manager/secretary — such person is also guilty.

question_html: Under Section 142, which court can take cognizance of an offence under Section 138, and what is the time limit for filing a complaint?

options.A: Any Court including a Civil Court — within 3 months of dishonour
options.B: The complaint must be made within ONE MONTH of the cause of action arising; only on a WRITTEN COMPLAINT by the PAYEE OR HOLDER IN DUE COURSE; no court INFERIOR TO A METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE OR JUDICIAL MAGISTRATE OF THE FIRST CLASS shall try such offence
options.C: The Criminal Court has 6 months within which to take cognizance automatically
options.D: Any Magistrate regardless of rank — within 6 months of the cheque presentation

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Any Court including a Civil Court — within 3 months of dishonour

Section 142: COGNIZANCE of offence under Section 138: (1) ONLY UPON A WRITTEN COMPLAINT by the PAYEE or HOLDER IN DUE COURSE; (2) Complaint must be made WITHIN ONE MONTH of the date on which the CAUSE OF ACTION ARISES (i.e., after 15 days from demand notice expire without payment); (3) Court may take cognizance after prescribed period if SUFFICIENT CAUSE is shown; (4) NO COURT INFERIOR TO A METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE OR JUDICIAL MAGISTRATE OF THE FIRST CLASS shall try such offence. Jurisdiction: where the cheque is delivered for collection — branch where PAYEE/HDC MAINTAINS ACCOUNT; or where presented directly — branch where DRAWER MAINTAINS ACCOUNT.

question_html: Under Section 143, all offences under Chapter XVII (Section 138 etc.) shall be tried by which court and what is the maximum fine in a SUMMARY TRIAL?

options.A: Sessions Court — fine up to Rs. 1 lakh
options.B: High Court — fine up to Rs. 5 lakhs
options.C: Judicial Magistrate of the First Class or Metropolitan Magistrate — in summary trial, maximum imprisonment = 1 year and fine EXCEEDING Rs. 5,000; trial should be concluded within 6 MONTHS from date of complaint
options.D: Any court of law — fine up to Rs. 10,000 without any time limit

answer_html:
Answer: (C) Judicial Magistrate of the First Class or Metropolitan Magistrate — in summary trial, maximum imprisonment = 1 year and fine EXCEEDING Rs. 5,000; trial should be concluded within 6 MONTHS from date of complaint

Section 143: ALL OFFENCES under Chapter XVII to be tried by a JUDICIAL MAGISTRATE OF FIRST CLASS or METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE. In SUMMARY TRIAL: maximum imprisonment = 1 YEAR; fine exceeding RS. 5,000. If the Magistrate finds that a sentence EXCEEDING 1 YEAR may be required — he shall convert to regular trial (recall witnesses). Trial shall be CONDUCTED FROM DAY TO DAY; adjournment only with recorded reasons. Endeavour to CONCLUDE TRIAL WITHIN 6 MONTHS from filing of complaint. Section 143A (2018 Amendment): interim compensation up to 20% of cheque value when drawer pleads 'not guilty'.

question_html: Under Section 146, for proceedings under Section 138, the court shall PRESUME which fact on production of the bank's slip or memo showing dishonour?

options.A: That the drawer had fraudulent intent when issuing the cheque
options.B: No presumption — the dishonour must be separately proved by the complainant
options.C: That the cheque has been VALIDLY DRAWN and there is a legal liability on the drawer
options.D: The FACT OF DISHONOUR of such cheque shall be PRESUMED — unless and until such fact is disproved — on production of bank's slip or memo having the OFFICIAL MARK denoting that the cheque has been dishonoured

answer_html:
Answer: (B) No presumption — the dishonour must be separately proved by the complainant

Section 146: The court shall, in respect of every proceeding, on production of BANK'S SLIP OR MEMO having thereon the OFFICIAL MARK DENOTING THAT THE CHEQUE HAS BEEN DISHONOURED, PRESUME THE FACT OF DISHONOUR of such cheque — unless and until such fact is DISPROVED. This evidential presumption saves the complainant from having to produce a bank officer to testify about dishonour — the dishonour slip serves as prima facie proof.
topic_text: Section 146 — Bank's Slip as Prima Facie Evidence

question_html: Under Section 147 of the NI Act, the offence under Section 138 (dishonour of cheque) is:

options.A: Non-compoundable — the court must always impose punishment
options.B: Compoundable only with the permission of the High Court
options.C: Compoundable — every offence punishable under the Act is compoundable
options.D: Compoundable only in summary proceedings — not in regular trials

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Non-compoundable — the court must always impose punishment

Section 147: EVERY OFFENCE PUNISHABLE UNDER THE NI ACT IS COMPOUNDABLE. Case: M. Rangaswamiah v. R. Shettappa (Karn HC, 2002): there is NO PROHIBITION against compounding of offence under Section 138; where the parties have settled and the complainant submits that the accused has paid the money, it is appropriate to allow compounding rather than inflict sentence — particularly since the offence is against a particular person (not society at large) to whom the sum is due. The court should facilitate settlement.

question_html: Under Section 80 of the NI Act, when NO RATE OF INTEREST is specified in the instrument, interest shall be calculated at what rate from the date of due to the date of realisation?

options.A: 12% per annum
options.B: 6% per annum
options.C: 18% per annum
options.D: The bank rate as fixed by the RBI

answer_html:
Answer: (C) 18% per annum

Section 79: Interest is payable on the amount paid AFTER THE DUE DATE — from the date of due to the date of realisation. Section 80: When NO INTEREST RATE IS SPECIFIED in the instrument, the interest shall be calculated at the rate of 18% PER ANNUM from the date of due to the date of realisation of the amount. This is the statutory default rate under the NI Act. Section 78: Payment should be made to the HOLDER or his ACCREDITED AGENT.

question_html: Under Section 84, where a CHEQUE IS NOT PRESENTED FOR PAYMENT WITHIN A REASONABLE TIME and the drawer suffers ACTUAL DAMAGE through the delay, the drawer is DISCHARGED:

options.A: Completely from all liability on the cheque
options.B: To the EXTENT OF SUCH DAMAGE — to the extent to which the drawer is a creditor of the banker to a larger amount than he would have been if the cheque had been paid within a reasonable time
options.C: Only if he can prove the payee was responsible for the delay
options.D: Only after giving 30 days' notice to the payee

answer_html:
Answer: (B) To the EXTENT OF SUCH DAMAGE — to the extent to which the drawer is a creditor of the banker to a larger amount than he would have been if the cheque had been paid within a reasonable time

Section 84: Where a cheque is NOT PRESENTED WITHIN A REASONABLE TIME and the drawer SUFFERS ACTUAL DAMAGE through the delay (e.g., the bank became insolvent during the delay), the drawer is DISCHARGED TO THE EXTENT OF SUCH DAMAGE (the extent he is a creditor of the banker to a LARGER AMOUNT than he would have been if the cheque had been timely presented). Case: Abdul Majid v. Ganesh Das (AIR 1954 Ori): drawer must prove (1) he had SUFFICIENT MONEY in bank; and (2) he SUFFERED ACTUAL DAMAGE from non-presentment within reasonable time.
topic_text: Section 84 — Delay in Presentation of Cheque

question_html: Under Section 120, what is the ESTOPPEL against the maker of a promissory note in a suit by a HOLDER IN DUE COURSE?

options.A: The maker is estopped from DENYING THE VALIDITY of the instrument as originally made
options.B: The maker is estopped from claiming any defect in the instrument after accepting payment
options.C: The maker is estopped from suing the payee for recovery of the amount
options.D: The maker is estopped from endorsing the instrument after creation

answer_html:
Answer: (A) The maker is estopped from DENYING THE VALIDITY of the instrument as originally made

Section 120: No MAKER OF A PROMISSORY NOTE, DRAWER OF A BILL/CHEQUE, or ACCEPTOR OF A BILL FOR THE HONOUR OF THE DRAWER shall, in a suit thereon by a HOLDER IN DUE COURSE, be permitted to DENY THE VALIDITY OF THE INSTRUMENT AS ORIGINALLY MADE OR DRAWN. Section 121: No MAKER OF PN or ACCEPTOR OF BoE payable to order shall deny the PAYEE'S CAPACITY at the date of the note or bill to INDORSE the same, in a suit by a HDC. Section 122: No INDORSER shall deny the SIGNATURE or CAPACITY TO CONTRACT of any PRIOR PARTY to the indorsement.

question_html: Under Section 137 of the NI Act, regarding foreign law applicable to negotiable instruments:

options.A: Foreign law always prevails over Indian law in all cases
options.B: The Indian courts apply only Indian law regardless of where the instrument was made
options.C: The law of any foreign country regarding promissory notes, bills of exchange and cheques shall be PRESUMED TO BE THE SAME AS THAT OF INDIA unless and until the contrary is proved
options.D: Foreign law applies only if the instrument is drawn payable in a foreign country

answer_html:
Answer: (C) The law of any foreign country regarding promissory notes, bills of exchange and cheques shall be PRESUMED TO BE THE SAME AS THAT OF INDIA unless and until the contrary is proved

Section 137: The LAW OF ANY FOREIGN COUNTRY regarding promissory notes, BoE and cheques shall be PRESUMED TO BE THE SAME AS THAT OF INDIA unless and until the CONTRARY IS PROVED. Section 134: The LIABILITY OF THE MAKER OR DRAWER of a foreign instrument is regulated by the law of the PLACE WHERE HE MADE IT; the liability of ACCEPTOR and INDORSER by the law of the PLACE WHERE THE INSTRUMENT IS MADE PAYABLE. Section 135: What constitutes dishonour and what notice of dishonour is sufficient is determined by the law of the PLACE WHERE IT IS MADE PAYABLE.

question_html: Under Section 43, a negotiable instrument made WITHOUT CONSIDERATION (or for a consideration which fails) creates no obligation between the immediate parties. However, if such party TRANSFERS IT to a HOLDER FOR CONSIDERATION, such holder may:

options.A: Not recover any amount — the absence of consideration is fatal to the entire instrument
options.B: RECOVER THE AMOUNT FROM THE TRANSFEROR FOR CONSIDERATION OR ANY PRIOR PARTY — the holder for consideration and every subsequent holder deriving title from him may recover the amount due
options.C: Only recover from the original maker — not from any endorser
options.D: Recover only if the transfer was accompanied by a written deed of assignment

answer_html:
Answer: (B) RECOVER THE AMOUNT FROM THE TRANSFEROR FOR CONSIDERATION OR ANY PRIOR PARTY — the holder for consideration and every subsequent holder deriving title from him may recover the amount due

Section 43: A negotiable instrument made WITHOUT CONSIDERATION or for a FAILING CONSIDERATION creates NO OBLIGATION between the immediate parties. But if such party TRANSFERS the instrument — with or without endorsement — to a HOLDER FOR CONSIDERATION, such holder and EVERY SUBSEQUENT HOLDER DERIVING TITLE from him may RECOVER THE AMOUNT from the TRANSFEROR FOR CONSIDERATION or any PRIOR PARTY. Explanation 1: No party for whose ACCOMMODATION an instrument was made, if he has paid, can recover from any accommodation party. Explanation 2: A party who INDUCED another to make an instrument for a consideration he FAILED TO PAY cannot recover more than the value of consideration actually paid. CONSOLIDATED ANSWER KEY — ALL 50 QUESTIONS — END OF QUESTION PAPER — Prepared from ICMAI Study Module | Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 | Module 4 | Syllabus 2022 | CMA Inter June 2026

question_html: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 applies to factories, mines, oilfields, plantations, ports, railway companies, shops or other establishments employing:

options.A: 5 or more persons with aid of power; 10 without aid of power
options.B: 10 or more persons (with aid of power); 20 (without aid of power)
options.C: 20 or more persons regardless of power usage
options.D: 25 or more persons in any establishment

answer_html:
Answer: (B) 10 or more persons (with aid of power); 20 (without aid of power)

The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 applies to factories, mines, oilfields, plantations, ports, railway companies, shops or other establishments employing 10 OR MORE PERSONS (with aid of power) and 20 (without aid of power). Once an establishment is covered, it continues to be covered even if the number falls below the threshold.

question_html: The Payment of Gratuity Rules, 1972, made by the Central Government to carry out the provisions of the Act, came into force with effect from:

options.A: 1st January 1972
options.B: 16th September 1972
options.C: 1st April 1972
options.D: 26th January 1973

answer_html:
Answer: (C) 1st April 1972

The Payment of Gratuity Rules, 1972 came into force with effect from 16TH SEPTEMBER 1972. The Act itself was enacted in 1972. The Rules provide the procedural framework for nomination, claims, applications, notices and payment under the Act.

question_html: Under Section 2(e) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, which of the following is EXCLUDED from the definition of 'employee'?

options.A: A person holding a post under the Central or State Government governed by another Act providing for gratuity
options.B: A teacher in a private educational institution
options.C: A worker employed in a mine
options.D: A worker employed in a plantation

answer_html:
Answer: (A) A person holding a post under the Central or State Government governed by another Act providing for gratuity

Section 2(e): Employee means any person (other than an apprentice) employed for wages in any kind of work in a covered establishment. EXCLUDED are: (a) APPRENTICES; and (b) persons HOLDING A POST UNDER CENTRAL OR STATE GOVERNMENT governed by any other Act or rules providing for payment of gratuity. Note: After the 2009 Amendment, TEACHERS in educational institutions are now included.

question_html: The Payment of Gratuity (Amendment) Act, 2009 expanded the definition of 'employee' to include which category of persons who were earlier excluded?

options.A: Government employees with separate pension rules
options.B: Teachers in educational institutions
options.C: Apprentices under the Apprentices Act, 1961
options.D: Members of the Armed Forces

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Teachers in educational institutions

Prior to the 2009 Amendment, the Supreme Court in Ahmedabad Private Primary Teachers Association v. Administrative Officer (AIR 2004 SC 1426) held that teachers were NOT employees under the Act. The PAYMENT OF GRATUITY (AMENDMENT) ACT, 2009 amended the definition of 'employee' to INCLUDE TEACHERS IN EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS within the purview of the Act.

question_html: Under Section 2(s) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 'wages' includes which of the following components?

options.A: Basic pay, dearness allowance, house rent allowance and commission
options.B: All emoluments earned while on duty or on leave paid in cash, AND dearness allowance
options.C: Basic pay, dearness allowance, bonus and overtime wages
options.D: All remuneration including house rent allowance and overtime wages

answer_html:
Answer: (C) Basic pay, dearness allowance, bonus and overtime wages

Section 2(s): Wages = all emoluments earned while on duty OR ON LEAVE in accordance with terms and conditions, paid or payable in cash, AND INCLUDES DEARNESS ALLOWANCE. It EXCLUDES: bonus, commission, house rent allowance, overtime wages, and any other allowance. Only DA is expressly included in wages for gratuity purposes.

question_html: What is the key distinction between 'retirement' [Section 2(q)] and 'superannuation' [Section 2(r)] under the Payment of Gratuity Act?

options.A: Retirement means termination of service otherwise than on superannuation; Superannuation means attaining the age fixed in the contract/conditions of service at which the employee shall vacate employment
options.B: Retirement and superannuation mean the same thing under the Act
options.C: Superannuation means voluntary resignation; retirement means compulsory termination by the employer
options.D: Retirement occurs only after 30 years of service; superannuation occurs after 60 years of age in all cases

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Retirement means termination of service otherwise than on superannuation; Superannuation means attaining the age fixed in the contract/conditions of service at which the employee shall vacate employment

Section 2(q): RETIREMENT = termination of service OTHERWISE THAN ON SUPERANNUATION. Section 2(r): SUPERANNUATION = in relation to an employee, the attainment of such age as is FIXED IN THE CONTRACT OR CONDITIONS OF SERVICE as the age on attaining which the employee shall vacate employment. Both trigger gratuity eligibility but the distinction is legally important.

question_html: Under Section 2(h), in the case of a MALE employee, 'family' for gratuity nomination purposes consists of:

options.A: Only wife and unmarried children
options.B: Himself, his wife, children (married or unmarried), dependent parents, dependent parents of his wife, and widow and children of his predeceased son
options.C: Wife, unmarried children, and parents only — no in-laws included
options.D: Wife, children, and parents — the widow of a predeceased son is excluded

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Himself, his wife, children (married or unmarried), dependent parents, dependent parents of his wife, and widow and children of his predeceased son

Section 2(h)(i): For a MALE EMPLOYEE, family includes: himself, his WIFE, his CHILDREN (whether married or unmarried), his DEPENDENT PARENTS, the DEPENDENT PARENTS OF HIS WIFE, and the WIDOW AND CHILDREN OF HIS PREDECEASED SON. Note: Adopted children are included where personal law permits adoption. A child given in adoption to another is excluded.

question_html: For an establishment having branches in more than one State, the 'appropriate Government' under the Payment of Gratuity Act is:

options.A: The State Government of the State where the head office is located
options.B: The State Government of each State for establishments in that State
options.C: The Central Government
options.D: Both Central and State Governments jointly

answer_html:
Answer: (C) The Central Government

Section 2(a): The CENTRAL GOVERNMENT is the appropriate government for: (i) establishments belonging to or under control of Central Government; (ii) establishments HAVING BRANCHES IN MORE THAN ONE STATE; (iii) factories belonging to or under control of Central Government; (iv) major ports, mines, oilfields, railway companies. For all other cases, the STATE GOVERNMENT is appropriate.

question_html: Under Section 5 of the Payment of Gratuity Act, the appropriate Government may exempt any establishment from the provisions of the Act if it is satisfied that:

options.A: Employees are in receipt of gratuity or pensionary benefits NOT LESS FAVOURABLE than the benefits under the Act
options.B: The establishment employs fewer than 10 persons
options.C: The establishment is a new enterprise less than 5 years old
options.D: The employer has registered with the controlling authority and paid a security deposit

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Employees are in receipt of gratuity or pensionary benefits NOT LESS FAVOURABLE than the benefits under the Act
