options.B: The Registrar shall INFORM THE AFFECTED PARTIES WITHIN 30 DAYS of making the entry in the register of charges
options.C: The Registrar shall seek court confirmation within 60 days
options.D: The Registrar shall publish notice in Official Gazette within 15 days

answer_html:
Answer: (A) No further action required — the entry is final and binding

Section 83(2): The REGISTRAR SHALL INFORM THE AFFECTED PARTIES WITHIN 30 DAYS of making the entry in the register of charges. AFFECTED PARTIES: These would include the company whose charge is being satisfied and the charge holder (creditor). This notification requirement ensures: (1) The company is aware that the Registrar has independently verified and recorded the satisfaction; (2) The charge holder is informed that their security interest has been formally discharged in the public records; (3) Both parties have an opportunity to object if the Registrar's entry is incorrect. Section 82(3): Section 82 shall NOT AFFECT the powers of the Registrar to make an entry under Section 83.

question_html: Under Section 82(2), when the Registrar enters a memorandum of satisfaction in the Register of Charges, in which FORM does he inform the company?

options.A: Form CHG-4 — the same form used for intimation
options.B: FORM CHG-5 — Registrar orders entry of memorandum of satisfaction in Register of Charges and informs the COMPANY in Form CHG-5
options.C: Form CHG-2 — the form used for registration of new charges
options.D: Form CHG-6 — the form used for receiver appointments

answer_html:
Answer: (B) FORM CHG-5 — Registrar orders entry of memorandum of satisfaction in Register of Charges and informs the COMPANY in Form CHG-5

Section 82(2): If no cause is shown by the charge holder (in response to the 14-day notice), the Registrar shall ORDER that a MEMORANDUM OF SATISFACTION shall be ENTERED IN THE REGISTER OF CHARGES and INFORM THE COMPANY that he has done so IN FORM CHG-5. FORMS SUMMARY for charge satisfaction: FORM CHG-4: Filed by COMPANY or CHARGE HOLDER to INTIMATE satisfaction to Registrar (within 300 days); FORM CHG-5: Issued BY REGISTRAR to the COMPANY confirming that a MEMORANDUM OF SATISFACTION has been entered. CHG-4 → (Registrar process: 14-day notice to charge holder) → CHG-5.

question_html: Which of the following correctly summarises the COMPLETE PROCESS for satisfaction (discharge) of a charge under the Companies Act, 2013?

options.A: Company files Form CHG-1 → Registrar issues Form CHG-2 → satisfaction complete
options.B: Company files Form CHG-4 within 30 days → Registrar issues Form CHG-5
options.C: Company/charge holder files FORM CHG-4 within 300 DAYS → Registrar gives 14-DAY NOTICE to charge holder (unless signed) → No cause shown: Registrar enters MEMORANDUM OF SATISFACTION in Register + informs company in FORM CHG-5 → Cause shown: Registrar records note → Section 83: Registrar may suo motu enter satisfaction; informs affected parties within 30 DAYS
options.D: Company files Form CHG-8 → CG approves → Registrar discharges charge

answer_html:
Answer: (C) Company/charge holder files FORM CHG-4 within 300 DAYS → Registrar gives 14-DAY NOTICE to charge holder (unless signed) → No cause shown: Registrar enters MEMORANDUM OF SATISFACTION in Register + informs company in FORM CHG-5 → Cause shown: Registrar records note → Section 83: Registrar may suo motu enter satisfaction; informs affected parties within 30 DAYS

COMPLETE SATISFACTION PROCESS: STEP 1: COMPANY OR CHARGE HOLDER files FORM CHG-4 within 300 DAYS of full payment/satisfaction. STEP 2: REGISTRAR gives 14-DAY NOTICE to the HOLDER OF CHARGE to show cause why satisfaction should not be recorded [EXCEPTION: No notice if charge holder signed the intimation]. STEP 3A (No cause shown): Registrar ORDERS MEMORANDUM OF SATISFACTION to be entered in Register; INFORMS COMPANY in FORM CHG-5. STEP 3B (Cause shown): Registrar RECORDS A NOTE in Register; INFORMS COMPANY. ALTERNATIVE ROUTE (Section 83): Registrar may suo motu enter memorandum of satisfaction on evidence received from any source, notwithstanding no intimation from company; must INFORM AFFECTED PARTIES WITHIN 30 DAYS. NOTICE OF CHARGE & PUBLIC REGISTERS — SECTIONS 80, 81, 85
topic_text: Satisfaction of Charge — Summary of Process

question_html: Under Section 80 of the Companies Act, 2013, when a charge is REGISTERED, what notice does it provide to third parties?

options.A: Only actual notice to parties who specifically searched the register
options.B: Notice only to existing shareholders and debenture holders
options.C: Any person ACQUIRING property, assets, undertakings, part thereof OR any SHARE OR INTEREST THEREIN shall be DEEMED TO HAVE NOTICE OF THE CHARGE from the DATE OF SUCH REGISTRATION — CONSTRUCTIVE NOTICE regardless of actual knowledge
options.D: Notice only to parties who acquired property after date of registration

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Only actual notice to parties who specifically searched the register

Section 80: CONSTRUCTIVE NOTICE OF CHARGE: Where any CHARGE on any property or assets of a company or any of its undertakings is REGISTERED — any person: (a) ACQUIRING such property, assets, undertakings or part thereof; OR (b) acquiring any SHARE OR INTEREST THEREIN — shall be DEEMED TO HAVE NOTICE OF THE CHARGE from the DATE OF SUCH REGISTRATION. KEY FEATURES: (1) Notice is DEEMED (constructive) — does NOT require actual knowledge; (2) Person acquiring property CANNOT claim they didn't know about the charge if it was registered; (3) The notice runs from the DATE OF REGISTRATION (not creation); (4) Applies to acquirers of property AND acquirers of shares/interests in the company. This makes the charge register system effective as a public disclosure mechanism.

question_html: Under Section 81, who maintains the REGISTER OF CHARGES, and how is it publicly accessible?

options.A: The company maintains the register — accessible only to members
options.B: SEBI maintains the register for listed companies
options.C: THE REGISTRAR shall keep register containing PARTICULARS OF ALL CHARGES; OPEN TO INSPECTION BY ANY PERSON on payment of fees; Rule 7(1): MCA PORTAL (www.mca.gov.in) particulars = DEEMED REGISTER OF CHARGES for Sec.81(1)
options.D: NCLT maintains the register — only through court orders

answer_html:
Answer: (B) SEBI maintains the register for listed companies

Section 81(1): THE REGISTRAR shall, IN RESPECT OF EVERY COMPANY, keep a REGISTER CONTAINING PARTICULARS OF THE CHARGES REGISTERED in such form and manner as prescribed. Section 81(2): This register shall be OPEN TO INSPECTION BY ANY PERSON on payment of such FEES AS MAY BE PRESCRIBED. KEY POINT [Rule 7(1)]: The PARTICULARS OF CHARGES MAINTAINED ON THE MCA PORTAL (www.mca.gov.in) shall be DEEMED TO BE THE REGISTER OF CHARGES for the purposes of Section 81(1). This digitisation means the charge register is effectively maintained electronically on the MCA portal, accessible to the public online. Compare: COMPANY'S OWN REGISTER (Section 85, Form CHG-7) is maintained at the registered office and is open to members and creditors WITHOUT FEE and to others on payment.

question_html: Under Section 85, every company must maintain its OWN REGISTER OF CHARGES. What are the requirements?

options.A: Only listed companies need to maintain own register of charges
options.B: EVERY COMPANY shall keep at REGISTERED OFFICE register of charges in FORM CHG-7; includes ALL CHARGES AND FLOATING CHARGES affecting property or assets; COPY OF INSTRUMENT CREATING CHARGE also kept at registered office; INSPECTION: MEMBERS/CREDITORS — WITHOUT FEE; OTHERS — on payment subject to REASONABLE RESTRICTIONS by articles
options.C: Only charges above Rs. 1 crore need to be entered
options.D: The company's register can be kept at any convenient location

answer_html:
Answer: (C) Only charges above Rs. 1 crore need to be entered

Section 85: COMPANY'S OWN REGISTER OF CHARGES — Requirements: (1) EVERY COMPANY must maintain it; (2) Location: REGISTERED OFFICE; (3) Form: FORM CHG-7; (4) Content: ALL CHARGES AND FLOATING CHARGES affecting any property or assets of the company OR ANY OF ITS UNDERTAKINGS — with all prescribed particulars; (5) Additionally: A COPY OF THE INSTRUMENT CREATING THE CHARGE shall also be kept at the registered office. INSPECTION RIGHTS: (a) ANY MEMBER OR CREDITOR — WITHOUT ANY PAYMENT OF FEES; (b) ANY OTHER PERSON — on payment of such fees as prescribed, SUBJECT TO SUCH REASONABLE RESTRICTIONS as the COMPANY MAY BY ITS ARTICLES IMPOSE. Both the Registrar's register (Section 81) and the company's own register (Section 85) are public records.
topic_text: Section 85 — Company's Own Register of Charges

question_html: Under Rule 7(1), the MCA portal (www.mca.gov.in) plays which role in the charge registration system?

options.A: It is an optional digital backup — the physical register is the primary register
options.B: It is only used for filing fee payments — not for maintaining the register
options.C: The PARTICULARS OF CHARGES maintained on MCA PORTAL (www.mca.gov.in) shall be DEEMED TO BE THE REGISTER OF CHARGES for purposes of Section 81(1) — effectively making the digital MCA portal the OFFICIAL REGISTER of charges
options.D: The MCA portal register only applies to listed companies

answer_html:
Answer: (A) It is an optional digital backup — the physical register is the primary register

Rule 7(1): The PARTICULARS OF CHARGES MAINTAINED ON THE MINISTRY OF CORPORATE AFFAIRS PORTAL (www.mca.gov.in) shall be DEEMED TO BE THE REGISTER OF CHARGES for the PURPOSES OF SECTION 81(1). This provision is significant because: (1) It DIGITISES the charge registration system — the MCA portal is the official register, not a physical register; (2) Any person can search the MCA portal to check if a company's property is subject to any charges; (3) The constructive notice under Section 80 effectively means 'check the MCA portal' before acquiring any property of a company; (4) The Registrar's maintenance obligation under Section 81(1) is fulfilled through the MCA portal.
topic_text: MCA Portal as Register of Charges

question_html: Under Section 84, when a person obtains an order for APPOINTMENT OF A RECEIVER OR MANAGER of property subject to a charge, what are the notification requirements?

options.A: Only the court needs to be notified — no requirement to inform company or Registrar
options.B: WITHIN 30 DAYS FROM DATE OF ORDER: notify COMPANY and REGISTRAR with copy of order/instrument in FORM CHG-6; APPOINTING PERSON also notifies Company and Registrar within 30 DAYS; Registrar registers particulars; on CEASING to hold appointment — receiver gives notice to Company and Registrar
options.C: Only SEBI needs to be notified within 15 days
options.D: Notification only required when receiver is from a financial institution

answer_html:
Answer: (B) WITHIN 30 DAYS FROM DATE OF ORDER: notify COMPANY and REGISTRAR with copy of order/instrument in FORM CHG-6; APPOINTING PERSON also notifies Company and Registrar within 30 DAYS; Registrar registers particulars; on CEASING to hold appointment — receiver gives notice to Company and Registrar

Section 84: DUAL NOTIFICATION OBLIGATION (within 30 days of order): (1) PERSON WHO OBTAINS ORDER (typically the charge holder/court): shall give notice to the COMPANY and the REGISTRAR along with a copy of the ORDER OR INSTRUMENT in FORM CHG-6; (2) PERSON WHO APPOINTS a receiver or authorised person: shall ALSO give notice to COMPANY and REGISTRAR within 30 DAYS with copy. Registrar: on payment of prescribed fees, shall REGISTER THE PARTICULARS of the receiver/person/instrument in the REGISTER OF CHARGES. CESSATION: The receiver/manager shall, ON CEASING TO HOLD SUCH APPOINTMENT, give notice to COMPANY AND REGISTRAR; Registrar shall REGISTER SUCH NOTICE. PENALTIES & FORMS — SECTION 86, ALL FORMS
topic_text: Section 84 — Appointment of Receiver or Manager

question_html: Under Section 86, if any company CONTRAVENES any provisions of Chapter VI (Registration of Charges), what is the penalty?

options.A: Only a warning letter — no financial penalty
options.B: Company: fine only up to Rs. 25,000; officers: no personal liability
options.C: COMPANY: fine NOT LESS THAN RS. 1 LAKH but may extend to RS. 10 LAKHS; EVERY DEFAULTING OFFICER: imprisonment up to 6 MONTHS or fine NOT LESS THAN RS. 25,000 but may extend to RS. 1 LAKH or BOTH
options.D: Company: fine only up to Rs. 5 lakhs; officers: fine only up to Rs. 50,000

answer_html:
Answer: (C) COMPANY: fine NOT LESS THAN RS. 1 LAKH but may extend to RS. 10 LAKHS; EVERY DEFAULTING OFFICER: imprisonment up to 6 MONTHS or fine NOT LESS THAN RS. 25,000 but may extend to RS. 1 LAKH or BOTH

Section 86: PENALTY FOR CONTRAVENING CHAPTER VI (Sections 77–87): COMPANY = fine NOT LESS THAN RS. 1 LAKH but which may extend to RS. 10 LAKHS. EVERY DEFAULTING OFFICER = punishable with IMPRISONMENT for a term which may extend to 6 MONTHS or with fine NOT LESS THAN RS. 25,000 but which may extend to RS. 1 LAKH or WITH BOTH. COMPARISON: This is a relatively modest penalty compared to deposits contravention (Section 76A: Rs.1Cr–10Cr for company; 7 years imprisonment for officer) — reflecting the civil nature of most charge registration violations.
topic_text: Section 86 — Penalty for Contravening Chapter VI

question_html: Under Section 86, for a contravention of Chapter VI, which persons are liable to be penalised?

options.A: Only the company — no individual officer is liable
options.B: THE COMPANY itself and EVERY OFFICER OF THE COMPANY WHO IS IN DEFAULT — both are liable; officer: imprisonment up to 6 months or fine Rs. 25,000 to Rs. 1 lakh or both
options.C: Only the managing director and company secretary
options.D: Only the charge holder — the company itself has no liability

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Only the company — no individual officer is liable

Section 86: BOTH the COMPANY AND EVERY OFFICER OF THE COMPANY WHO IS IN DEFAULT are liable. COMPANY: fine Rs. 1 LAKH to Rs. 10 LAKHS. EVERY DEFAULTING OFFICER: imprisonment up to 6 MONTHS OR fine Rs. 25,000 to Rs. 1 LAKH OR BOTH. The term 'officer in default' under Companies Act typically includes managing director, whole-time director, manager, company secretary, and any director who is aware of the default and consented to it. The dual liability (company + officers) reflects the principle that corporate compliance obligations fall on both the entity and the responsible individuals.

question_html: Which of the following correctly matches the FORMS with their purpose under the Companies (Registration of Charges) Rules, 2014?

options.A: CHG-1: Certificate of creation; CHG-2: Application for registration; CHG-3: Certificate of satisfaction
options.B: CHG-1: Application for REGISTRATION (non-debenture)/CONDONATION; CHG-2: CERTIFICATE OF REGISTRATION; CHG-3: CERTIFICATE OF MODIFICATION; CHG-4: INTIMATION OF SATISFACTION (by company/charge holder); CHG-5: MEMORANDUM OF SATISFACTION (issued by Registrar); CHG-6: Notice of RECEIVER/MANAGER; CHG-7: COMPANY'S OWN REGISTER; CHG-8: Application to CENTRAL GOVERNMENT for condonation; CHG-9: Application for DEBENTURE CHARGES
options.C: All forms are used only for charge creation
options.D: CHG-4: Certificate of registration; CHG-5: Application for satisfaction

answer_html:
Answer: (B) CHG-1: Application for REGISTRATION (non-debenture)/CONDONATION; CHG-2: CERTIFICATE OF REGISTRATION; CHG-3: CERTIFICATE OF MODIFICATION; CHG-4: INTIMATION OF SATISFACTION (by company/charge holder); CHG-5: MEMORANDUM OF SATISFACTION (issued by Registrar); CHG-6: Notice of RECEIVER/MANAGER; CHG-7: COMPANY'S OWN REGISTER; CHG-8: Application to CENTRAL GOVERNMENT for condonation; CHG-9: Application for DEBENTURE CHARGES

COMPLETE FORMS CHART for Chapter VI: CHG-1: Application for CREATION/CONDONATION of non-debenture charges (by company or condonation application); CHG-2: CERTIFICATE OF REGISTRATION OF CHARGE (issued by Registrar — conclusive evidence); CHG-3: CERTIFICATE OF MODIFICATION OF CHARGE (issued by Registrar); CHG-4: INTIMATION OF SATISFACTION of charge (filed by company or charge holder within 300 days); CHG-5: MEMORANDUM OF SATISFACTION (issued by Registrar after 14-day notice process); CHG-6: Notice of APPOINTMENT or CESSATION of RECEIVER or MANAGER; CHG-7: COMPANY'S OWN REGISTER of charges (maintained at registered office); CHG-8: Application for CONDONATION OF DELAY TO CENTRAL GOVERNMENT (beyond 300 days); CHG-9: Application for registration of DEBENTURE charges (securing issue of debentures); INC-28: Filing of CG's condonation ORDER with Registrar [Rule 12(3)].
topic_text: Complete Forms List — Chapter VI (Registration of Charges)

question_html: Under the Companies Act, 2013, what is a FLOATING CHARGE and how does it differ from a FIXED CHARGE?

options.A: Floating charges are not recognised under the Companies Act
options.B: A FLOATING CHARGE HOVERS OVER A CLASS OF ASSETS that fluctuate in ordinary business (stock, book debts, inventory) — crystallises into FIXED CHARGE on specified events (winding up, default, receiver appointment); a FIXED CHARGE is on SPECIFIC IDENTIFIED ASSETS; BOTH MUST BE REGISTERED under Section 77
options.C: Floating charges only on immovable property; fixed charges on moveable assets
options.D: A floating charge means the charge amount changes daily

answer_html:
Answer: (C) Floating charges only on immovable property; fixed charges on moveable assets

FIXED CHARGE vs FLOATING CHARGE: FIXED CHARGE: Created on SPECIFIC IDENTIFIED ASSETS (e.g., a specific building, a specific piece of machinery); the company CANNOT deal with the asset without the charge holder's consent; e.g., a mortgage on a factory. FLOATING CHARGE: Created on a CLASS OF ASSETS that fluctuate in the ORDINARY COURSE OF BUSINESS (e.g., stock-in-trade, book debts, debtors, inventory); the company CAN deal with the assets in the ordinary course (buy/sell stock) until CRYSTALLISATION; CRYSTALLISATION occurs on: (a) WINDING UP; (b) DEFAULT and demand; (c) APPOINTMENT OF RECEIVER. Section 85: Both CHARGES AND FLOATING CHARGES must be included in the company's own register. Both types must be registered with the Registrar under Section 77.

question_html: Under Section 77(1), the Central Government in consultation with the RBI may prescribe charges that are EXEMPT from registration. What is the significance of this exemption?

options.A: All charges are exempt if the company is a banking company
options.B: Charges on property in foreign countries are always exempt
options.C: The Section empowers CG (in consultation with RBI) to exempt SPECIFIED TYPES OF CHARGES from registration — typically covering financial sector charges already regulated under RBI Act/Banking Regulation Act; prevents duplication of regulatory requirements
options.D: Only charges created before 2013 are exempt

answer_html:
Answer: (A) All charges are exempt if the company is a banking company

Section 77(1): 'THIS SECTION SHALL NOT APPLY TO SUCH CHARGES AS MAY BE PRESCRIBED IN CONSULTATION WITH THE RESERVE BANK OF INDIA.' SIGNIFICANCE: This allows the CG to exempt certain financial sector charges that are already subject to RBI regulation (e.g., charges under SARFAESI Act, certain banking charges). The exemption prevents: (1) Duplication of regulatory burden; (2) Conflicting disclosure requirements under different laws; (3) Administrative overload for companies that are already complying with equivalent disclosure requirements under other regulatory frameworks. The consultation with RBI ensures that banking and financial sector interests are protected when granting exemptions.

question_html: A company creates a charge on its factory building (immovable property) on 1st January 2025. It fails to register the charge within 30 days. It applies to the Registrar for condonation on 1st March 2025 (59th day). Is this application within the permissible first condonation period?

options.A: No — the 30-day period has expired and no further extension is available
options.B: YES — Rule 4(1) allows condonation within 120 DAYS of creation; 59th day is within 120 days; application in Form CHG-1 with declaration from CS/Director; payment of additional fee
options.C: Yes — but only if delay was due to force majeure
options.D: No — Registrar has no power to condone delays; only CG can

answer_html:
Answer: (B) YES — Rule 4(1) allows condonation within 120 DAYS of creation; 59th day is within 120 days; application in Form CHG-1 with declaration from CS/Director; payment of additional fee

CASE ANALYSIS: Charge created: 1st January 2025; Normal 30-day period expires: 31st January 2025; Application made: 1st March 2025 (Day 59 from creation). Rule 4(1): Registrar may allow first condonation within a period of 120 DAYS of creation. Since Day 59 is WITHIN 120 DAYS, the application IS TIMELY for first condonation. REQUIREMENTS: (1) Company must satisfy the Registrar of SUFFICIENT CAUSE for not filing within 30 days; (2) Application in FORM CHG-1; (3) Declaration from SECRETARY OR DIRECTOR that belated filing shall NOT ADVERSELY AFFECT RIGHTS OF ANY INTERVENING CREDITORS; (4) PAYMENT OF ADDITIONAL FEE. If the application had been made on Day 121 or later (e.g., 1st May 2025), the first condonation window would have closed and the company would need the Section 77 second extension (up to 300 days).
topic_text: Practical Application — Charge Registration in Case Scenario

question_html: A charge is created on 1st April 2024. The company registers the charge only on 1st August 2024 (Day 122). On what basis may the Registrar accept this registration?

options.A: The Registrar cannot accept this — registration must be within 30 days in all cases
options.B: This is within the first condonation period — company can use Rule 4(1)
options.C: DAY 122 IS BETWEEN DAYS 121 AND 300 — Registrar may allow registration within 300 DAYS of creation on payment of ADDITIONAL FEES (SECOND EXTENSION under Section 77); subsequent registration shall NOT PREJUDICE rights acquired BEFORE actual registration
options.D: Day 122 falls outside all permissible windows — only CG can allow

answer_html:
Answer: (C) DAY 122 IS BETWEEN DAYS 121 AND 300 — Registrar may allow registration within 300 DAYS of creation on payment of ADDITIONAL FEES (SECOND EXTENSION under Section 77); subsequent registration shall NOT PREJUDICE rights acquired BEFORE actual registration

CASE ANALYSIS: Charge created: 1st April 2024; Registration attempted: 1st August 2024 = DAY 122 from creation. TIME WINDOW ANALYSIS: 0–30 days: NORMAL (expired on 30th April 2024); 31–120 days: FIRST CONDONATION Rule 4(1) (expired approximately on 30th July 2024); 121–300 days: SECOND EXTENSION by Registrar on Section 77 application (Day 121 to Day 300). Since Day 122 falls in the SECOND EXTENSION window (121–300 days): The REGISTRAR may, on APPLICATION BY THE COMPANY, allow registration within 300 DAYS on PAYMENT OF ADDITIONAL FEES. IMPORTANT: Subsequent registration shall NOT PREJUDICE rights acquired BEFORE actual registration (1st August 2024). Any creditor who extended credit or acquired rights over the property between 1st April and 1st August 2024 is protected.

question_html: Bank A creates a charge on a factory on 1st January 2025 but fails to register it. Bank B also creates a charge on the same factory on 15th February 2025 and immediately registers it. What is the priority of the two charges?

options.A: Bank A's charge has priority being earlier in time — regardless of registration
options.B: BANK B'S REGISTERED CHARGE TAKES PRIORITY over Bank A's unregistered charge — Bank B had no notice (constructive or otherwise) of Bank A's unregistered charge; Section 77(3): Bank A's unregistered charge cannot be 'taken into account' by any other creditor (Bank B); Bank B's charge, being duly registered, is fully enforceable
options.C: Both charges have equal priority regardless of registration
options.D: The later charge (Bank B) always takes priority since it was registered first

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Bank A's charge has priority being earlier in time — regardless of registration

PRIORITY ANALYSIS: BANK A: Charge created 1st January 2025 — UNREGISTERED. BANK B: Charge created 15th February 2025 — REGISTERED. LEGAL POSITION: Section 77(3): No charge shall be TAKEN INTO ACCOUNT by any OTHER CREDITOR unless it is duly registered. Section 80: Constructive notice only arises from the DATE OF REGISTRATION. Since Bank A's charge is NOT REGISTERED: (1) Bank B had NO CONSTRUCTIVE NOTICE of Bank A's charge when it created its own charge; (2) Under Section 77(3), Bank A's unregistered charge CANNOT be 'taken into account' by Bank B (as 'any other creditor'); (3) BANK B'S REGISTERED CHARGE TAKES PRIORITY. Bank A retains its right to claim the DEBT (under Section 77(4)) but as an UNSECURED CREDITOR — it loses its priority as secured creditor over Bank B.
topic_text: Effect of Charge Registration on Other Creditors

question_html: Under Section 77(1), which types of INTANGIBLE PROPERTY are covered under the charge registration requirements?

options.A: No intangible property charges need to be registered — only tangible assets are covered
options.B: Only patents and trademarks — other intangibles are exempt
options.C: Section 77 explicitly covers BOTH TANGIBLE AND INTANGIBLE PROPERTY; intangibles include: GOODWILL, PATENTS, TRADE MARKS, LICENCES, INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY RIGHTS, BOOK DEBTS — all charges on intangible assets must be registered
options.D: Intangible property charges registered only if value exceeds Rs. 10 crores

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Only patents and trademarks — other intangibles are exempt

Section 77(1): The properties may be TANGIBLE OR INTANGIBLE. INTANGIBLE PROPERTY CHARGES requiring registration include: (1) GOODWILL of the business; (2) PATENTS and their licences; (3) TRADE MARKS; (4) BOOK DEBTS (present and future receivables); (5) COPYRIGHTS; (6) LICENCES; (7) Other intellectual property rights. The inclusion of intangible property is increasingly important in modern business where companies' most valuable assets are often intellectual property, brand value, and receivables. A lender taking security on a company's patent portfolio or brand name must ensure the charge is registered with the Registrar to protect its security.

question_html: Which of the following CORRECTLY summarises the key provisions and forms of Chapter VI (Registration of Charges)?

options.A: Only immovable property charges need registration; only one form (CHG-1); no time limits
options.B: Registration is optional; company may choose whether to register
options.C: Registration required for ALL CHARGES (Sec.77); 30-day time limit; CHG-1/CHG-9; Certificate CHG-2 (conclusive evidence); Modification Sec.79 (CHG-3); Charge holder registration Sec.78 (14-day notice, fee recovery); Constructive notice Sec.80; Registrar's register MCA portal Sec.81; Satisfaction CHG-4 (300 days) → 14-day notice → CHG-5; Sec.83 suo motu; Receiver notice CHG-6 (30 days); Company register CHG-7 Sec.85; CG condonation CHG-8; Penalty Sec.86 (Rs.1L–10L company; 6 months/Rs.25K–1L officer)
options.D: Registration required only for secured debentures; no penalty; void only after 2 years

answer_html:
Answer: (C) Registration required for ALL CHARGES (Sec.77); 30-day time limit; CHG-1/CHG-9; Certificate CHG-2 (conclusive evidence); Modification Sec.79 (CHG-3); Charge holder registration Sec.78 (14-day notice, fee recovery); Constructive notice Sec.80; Registrar's register MCA portal Sec.81; Satisfaction CHG-4 (300 days) → 14-day notice → CHG-5; Sec.83 suo motu; Receiver notice CHG-6 (30 days); Company register CHG-7 Sec.85; CG condonation CHG-8; Penalty Sec.86 (Rs.1L–10L company; 6 months/Rs.25K–1L officer)

COMPREHENSIVE SUMMARY of Chapter VI: SECTION 77: Duty to register ALL CHARGES within 30 days; Form CHG-1 (non-debenture), CHG-9 (debentures); Certificate CHG-2 (CONCLUSIVE EVIDENCE); unregistered charge VOID against liquidator/creditors (Sec.77(3)) but debt remains (Sec.77(4)); condonation: Rule 4 (120 days) → 300 days → CG (CHG-8). SECTION 78: Charge holder can register; 14-day notice to company; fee recovery from company. SECTION 79: Modification/acquired property charges; Certificate CHG-3. SECTION 80: Constructive notice from date of registration. SECTION 81: Registrar's register on MCA portal; open to any person. SECTIONS 82-83: Satisfaction process (CHG-4 within 300 days → 14-day notice → CHG-5); suo motu (Sec.83); inform affected parties in 30 days. SECTION 84: Receiver/manager notice (CHG-6) within 30 days. SECTION 85: Company's own register (CHG-7); members/creditors free. SECTION 86: Penalty Rs.1L–10L (company); 6 months/Rs.25K–1L (officer). SECTION 87: CG power to rectify/extend. CONSOLIDATED ANSWER KEY — ALL 50 QUESTIONS — END OF QUESTION PAPER — Prepared from ICMAI Study Module | Registration of Charges | Companies Act, 2013 — Chapter VI | Module 12.1 | Syllabus 2022 | CMA Inter June 2026

question_html: Under Section 4(3) of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, a contract is called an 'Agreement to Sell' when:

options.A: The buyer pays the price immediately but delivery is deferred
options.B: The transfer of property in goods is to take place at a future time or subject to some condition thereafter to be fulfilled
options.C: The seller transfers ownership immediately along with physical delivery
options.D: The contract is made orally without any written document

answer_html:
Answer: (B) The transfer of property in goods is to take place at a future time or subject to some condition thereafter to be fulfilled

Section 4(3): Where under a contract of sale the TRANSFER OF PROPERTY IN GOODS is to take place AT A FUTURE TIME or SUBJECT TO SOME CONDITION THEREAFTER TO BE FULFILLED, the contract is called an AGREEMENT TO SELL. Section 4(4): An agreement to sell becomes a SALE when the time elapses or the conditions are fulfilled. A sale is an executed contract; an agreement to sell is an executory contract.
topic_text: Section 4 — Contract of Sale vs Agreement to Sell

question_html: Which of the following correctly states an ESSENTIAL condition for a valid contract of sale under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930?

options.A: The goods must be in writing and must be registered
options.B: The contract must be between at least three parties
options.C: The consideration must be a definite price (money) and not an exchange of goods
options.D: The goods must be ascertained at the time of the contract

answer_html:
Answer: (C) The consideration must be a definite price (money) and not an exchange of goods

ESSENTIAL CONDITIONS of a contract of sale: (i) Two parties; (ii) Transfer of title/ownership; (iii) Subject matter must be GOODS (moveable property); (iv) CONSIDERATION must be a DESIGNATED AMOUNT PAYABLE IN MONEY (price) — not an exchange of goods. A contract of sale may be in writing, word of mouth, partly in writing, or implied from conduct of parties [Section 5].
topic_text: Section 4 — Contract of Sale: Essential Element

question_html: Under Section 2(7) of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, 'goods' means every kind of moveable property other than actionable claims and money. Which of the following is INCLUDED in 'goods'?

options.A: Stock and shares, growing crops, grass, and things attached to land agreed to be severed before sale
options.B: Actionable claims such as debts
options.C: Current coins and currency notes
options.D: Immovable property like buildings

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Stock and shares, growing crops, grass, and things attached to land agreed to be severed before sale

Section 2(7): GOODS = every kind of MOVEABLE PROPERTY other than ACTIONABLE CLAIMS and MONEY; and INCLUDES: STOCK AND SHARES, GROWING CROPS, GRASS, and THINGS ATTACHED TO OR FORMING PART OF THE LAND which are agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale. Money and actionable claims are excluded. Goodwill is included as it is a moveable property.

question_html: Under Section 5, a contract of sale may be made in which of the following forms?

options.A: Only in writing — oral contracts for sale of goods are not valid
options.B: In writing, or by word of mouth, or partly in writing and partly by word of mouth, or implied from the conduct of the parties
options.C: Only in writing if the price exceeds Rs. 500
options.D: Only in writing with attestation by two witnesses

answer_html:
Answer: (B) In writing, or by word of mouth, or partly in writing and partly by word of mouth, or implied from the conduct of the parties

Section 5: Subject to provisions of any law for the time being in force, a contract of sale may be made: (a) IN WRITING; OR (b) BY WORD OF MOUTH; OR (c) PARTLY IN WRITING AND PARTLY BY WORD OF MOUTH; OR (d) IMPLIED FROM THE CONDUCT OF THE PARTIES. The Act does NOT require contracts of sale to be in writing — they can be made in any of these four modes.
topic_text: Section 5 — How Contract of Sale is Made

question_html: Under Section 6(3) of the Sale of Goods Act, where a seller purports to effect a present sale of FUTURE GOODS, the contract operates as:

options.A: A void agreement — future goods cannot be the subject of a contract
options.B: A valid sale with immediate transfer of property
options.C: An agreement to sell the goods (not a completed sale)
options.D: A conditional sale subject to subsequent confirmation

answer_html:
Answer: (C) An agreement to sell the goods (not a completed sale)

Section 6(3): Where by a contract of sale the seller PURPORTS TO EFFECT A PRESENT SALE OF FUTURE GOODS, the contract OPERATES AS AN AGREEMENT TO SELL THE GOODS. Future goods means goods to be MANUFACTURED OR PRODUCED OR ACQUIRED by the seller AFTER THE MAKING OF THE CONTRACT of sale. Example: Ramcharan contracting in January to buy Bholu's potatoes from June harvest — these are future goods operating as agreement to sell.

question_html: Under Section 7, where there is a contract for the sale of specific goods and the goods, WITHOUT THE KNOWLEDGE OF THE SELLER, have PERISHED OR BECOME DAMAGED at the time of making the contract, the contract is:

options.A: Void — the subject matter ceases to exist before the contract is made
options.B: Voidable at the option of the seller
options.C: Valid — risk passes to the buyer on entering the contract
options.D: Enforceable if the seller later acquires similar goods

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Void — the subject matter ceases to exist before the contract is made

Section 7: Where there is a contract for the sale of SPECIFIC GOODS, the contract is VOID if the goods WITHOUT THE KNOWLEDGE OF THE SELLER have, AT THE TIME WHEN THE CONTRACT WAS MADE, PERISHED OR BECOME SO DAMAGED as no longer to answer to their description in the contract. The subject matter ceases to exist even before the contract, making it void ab-initio. Contrast with Section 8 (perishing after agreement to sell — agreement avoided).

question_html: Under Section 8, where there is an agreement to sell SPECIFIC GOODS and the goods perish WITHOUT FAULT OF EITHER PARTY before the risk passes to the buyer, the agreement is:

options.A: Enforceable — the seller must procure substitute goods
options.B: Thereby avoided (automatically cancelled)
options.C: Voidable at the buyer's option
options.D: Treated as a novation with new goods

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Thereby avoided (automatically cancelled)

Section 8: Where there is an AGREEMENT TO SELL SPECIFIC GOODS, and subsequently the goods WITHOUT ANY FAULT ON THE PART OF THE SELLER OR BUYER PERISH OR BECOME SO DAMAGED as no longer to answer to their description, BEFORE THE RISK PASSES TO THE BUYER, the agreement is THEREBY AVOIDED. This is distinct from Section 7 (void contract before agreement). The loss falls on the seller as risk has not yet passed to the buyer.
topic_text: Section 8 — Goods Perishing After Agreement to Sell

question_html: Under Section 9, where the price in a contract of sale has NOT been fixed by the contract or by the parties, the buyer shall pay:

options.A: The market price of the goods on the date of contract
options.B: The price fixed by the appropriate Government
options.C: A reasonable price, determined based on the relevant circumstances of each particular case
options.D: The price determined by an arbitrator appointed by the court

answer_html:
Answer: (C) A reasonable price, determined based on the relevant circumstances of each particular case

Section 9: The price in a contract of sale has to be FIXED BY THE CONTRACT ITSELF or be fixed in a MANNER AGREED BETWEEN THE PARTIES or determined by their COURSE OF DEALING. Where the price has NOT been so determined, the BUYER SHALL PAY THE SELLER A REASONABLE PRICE — determined based on the RELEVANT CIRCUMSTANCES of each particular case. 'Reasonable price' is flexible and fact-specific.

question_html: Under Section 10(1), where there is an agreement to sell goods at a price to be fixed by valuation of a THIRD PARTY who CANNOT OR DOES NOT MAKE SUCH VALUATION, the agreement is:

options.A: Avoided — but if goods have been delivered and appropriated by the buyer, he shall pay a reasonable price
options.B: Void ab-initio with no obligation on either party
options.C: Enforceable at the price last agreed upon by the parties
options.D: Voidable at the option of the seller only

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Avoided — but if goods have been delivered and appropriated by the buyer, he shall pay a reasonable price

Section 10(1): Where goods are to be sold at a price fixed by a THIRD-PARTY VALUATION and the third party CANNOT OR DOES NOT MAKE SUCH VALUATION, the agreement is THEREBY AVOIDED. EXCEPTION: If the goods or any part have been DELIVERED TO AND APPROPRIATED BY THE BUYER, he shall pay a REASONABLE PRICE. Section 10(2): If the third party is PREVENTED FROM MAKING VALUATION BY THE FAULT OF EITHER PARTY, the party NOT IN FAULT may SUE FOR DAMAGES against the party in fault.

question_html: Under Section 11, unless a different intention appears from the terms of the contract, stipulations as to TIME OF PAYMENT in a contract of sale are:

options.A: Always deemed to be of the essence of the contract
options.B: NOT deemed to be of the essence of a contract of sale
options.C: Of the essence only if stated in writing
options.D: Of the essence only if the goods are perishable

answer_html:
Answer: (B) NOT deemed to be of the essence of a contract of sale

Section 11: Unless a DIFFERENT INTENTION APPEARS from the terms of the contract, STIPULATIONS AS TO TIME OF PAYMENT are NOT DEEMED TO BE OF THE ESSENCE of a contract of sale. Whether any OTHER STIPULATION AS TO TIME is of the essence of the contract depends on the TERMS OF THE CONTRACT. This means a buyer's delay in payment alone does not normally give the seller the right to repudiate the contract. TRANSFER OF OWNERSHIP — SECTIONS 18–26

question_html: Under Section 18 of the Sale of Goods Act, in a contract for sale of UNASCERTAINED GOODS, the property in the goods passes to the buyer:

options.A: When the contract is entered into
options.B: When payment is made in full
options.C: Only when and until the goods are ASCERTAINED
options.D: Only when the goods are physically delivered

answer_html:
Answer: (C) Only when and until the goods are ASCERTAINED

Section 18: In a contract for the sale of UNASCERTAINED GOODS, the PROPERTY IN THE GOODS DOES NOT PASS TO THE BUYER UNLESS AND UNTIL THE GOODS ARE ASCERTAINED. This is the first and fundamental rule for passing of property. Ascertainment means the goods are identified and separated from the bulk specifically for the contract. Until ascertainment, no property passes regardless of other circumstances.

question_html: Under Section 20, in an UNCONDITIONAL CONTRACT for the sale of SPECIFIC GOODS in a DELIVERABLE STATE, when does property pass to the buyer?

options.A: When the property in goods is transferred to the buyer at such time as the parties to the contract intend it to be transferred — even if payment or delivery is postponed
options.B: Only when payment is made
options.C: Only when physical delivery takes place
options.D: Only when the buyer inspects and approves the goods

answer_html:
Answer: (A) When the property in goods is transferred to the buyer at such time as the parties to the contract intend it to be transferred — even if payment or delivery is postponed

Section 20: In an UNCONDITIONAL CONTRACT for the sale of SPECIFIC GOODS IN A DELIVERABLE STATE, the property passes to the buyer WHEN THE CONTRACT IS MADE — it is IMMATERIAL whether the TIME OF PAYMENT or the TIME OF DELIVERY (or both) is POSTPONED. Goods are in a 'DELIVERABLE STATE' when in such state that the buyer would under the contract be bound to take delivery of them.
topic_text: Section 20 — Specific Goods in Deliverable State

question_html: Under Section 21, where a contract is for the sale of specific goods and the seller is bound to do something to put them into a DELIVERABLE STATE, when does property pass?

options.A: When the contract is signed by both parties
options.B: When the seller has done that thing AND the buyer has notice thereof
options.C: When payment is made regardless of delivery state
options.D: When the buyer takes physical possession of the goods

answer_html:
Answer: (B) When the seller has done that thing AND the buyer has notice thereof

Section 21: Where there is a contract for the sale of specific goods and the SELLER IS BOUND TO DO SOMETHING to the goods for the purpose of PUTTING THEM INTO A DELIVERABLE STATE, the property DOES NOT PASS UNTIL: (a) SUCH THING IS DONE; AND (b) THE BUYER HAS NOTICE THEREOF. Both conditions — the act being done AND the buyer being notified — must be satisfied before property passes.
topic_text: Section 21 — Specific Goods Not in Deliverable State

question_html: Under Section 22, if specific goods are in a deliverable state but the seller must WEIGH, MEASURE, TEST or do something to ASCERTAIN THE PRICE, when does property pass?

options.A: When the contract is made
options.B: When payment is made
options.C: When such act or thing is done AND the buyer has notice thereof
options.D: When the seller communicates the price to the buyer

answer_html:
Answer: (C) When such act or thing is done AND the buyer has notice thereof

Section 22: In a contract for specific goods in a deliverable state, where the seller is bound to WEIGH, MEASURE, TEST or do some other act to ASCERTAIN THE PRICE, the property DOES NOT PASS UNTIL: (a) SUCH ACT OR THING IS DONE; AND (b) THE BUYER HAS NOTICE THEREOF. The buyer must be notified — the seller completing the act alone is insufficient to pass property.

question_html: Under Section 23, for unascertained or future goods sold by description, property passes when goods of that description are:

options.A: Unconditionally appropriated to the contract either by the seller (with assent of buyer) or by the buyer (with assent of seller) — assent may be expressed or implied
options.B: Only when physically delivered to the buyer
options.C: Only when specific goods matching the description are set aside privately by the seller
options.D: When payment is made in full

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Unconditionally appropriated to the contract either by the seller (with assent of buyer) or by the buyer (with assent of seller) — assent may be expressed or implied

Section 23: Where there is a contract for unascertained or future goods by description and goods of that description in a DELIVERABLE STATE are UNCONDITIONALLY APPROPRIATED to the contract — either by the SELLER WITH ASSENT OF THE BUYER or by the BUYER WITH ASSENT OF THE SELLER — the property passes. The ASSENT may be EXPRESS OR IMPLIED and may be given BEFORE OR AFTER THE APPROPRIATION. Section 23(2): Delivery to carrier WITHOUT RESERVING RIGHT OF DISPOSAL = unconditional appropriation.

question_html: Under Section 24, when goods are delivered to the buyer 'ON APPROVAL or ON SALE OR RETURN', property passes to the buyer when:

options.A: Only when the goods are physically delivered to the buyer's premises
options.B: (i) When he signifies his approval/acceptance; OR (ii) when he does any act adopting the transaction; OR (iii) when he retains goods beyond the fixed/reasonable time without giving notice of rejection
options.C: When the seller sends the invoice to the buyer
options.D: When half the price is paid as advance

answer_html:
Answer: (B) (i) When he signifies his approval/acceptance; OR (ii) when he does any act adopting the transaction; OR (iii) when he retains goods beyond the fixed/reasonable time without giving notice of rejection

Section 24: Property in goods ON APPROVAL or SALE OR RETURN passes when: (a) he SIGNIFIES HIS APPROVAL OR ACCEPTANCE to the seller; (b) he does any OTHER ACT ADOPTING THE TRANSACTION; or (c) if he DOES NOT SIGNIFY APPROVAL but RETAINS THE GOODS without giving notice of rejection — then if a TIME HAS BEEN FIXED, on EXPIRATION OF THAT TIME; if NO TIME IS FIXED, on EXPIRATION OF A REASONABLE TIME.
topic_text: Section 24 — Goods on Approval / Sale or Return

question_html: Under Section 25(2), where goods are shipped and by the BILL OF LADING the goods are deliverable to the ORDER OF THE SELLER or his agent, the seller is:

options.A: Deemed to have transferred ownership to the buyer
options.B: Obligated to endorse the bill of lading immediately
options.C: PRIMA FACIE DEEMED TO RESERVE THE RIGHT OF DISPOSAL of the goods
options.D: Deemed to have waived his right of lien over the goods

answer_html:
Answer: (C) PRIMA FACIE DEEMED TO RESERVE THE RIGHT OF DISPOSAL of the goods

Section 25(2): Where goods are SHIPPED or DELIVERED TO A RAILWAY ADMINISTRATION and by the BILL OF LADING or RAILWAY RECEIPT the goods are DELIVERABLE TO THE ORDER OF THE SELLER or his agent, the seller is PRIMA FACIE DEEMED TO RESERVE THE RIGHT OF DISPOSAL. Section 25(3): If the buyer does NOT HONOUR THE BILL OF EXCHANGE, he must RETURN the bill of lading or railway receipt; if he wrongfully retains it, PROPERTY IN GOODS DOES NOT PASS to him.
topic_text: Section 25 — Reservation of Right of Disposal

question_html: Under Section 26, the general rule about risk in a contract of sale is:

options.A: Risk passes when payment is made regardless of property ownership
options.B: Risk remains with the buyer from the moment the contract is entered into
options.C: Goods remain at the seller's risk until property is transferred to the buyer; once transferred, goods are at buyer's risk whether delivery has been made or not
options.D: Risk always remains with the party in physical possession of the goods

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Risk passes when payment is made regardless of property ownership

Section 26: Unless OTHERWISE AGREED, goods remain at the SELLER'S RISK until the property therein is TRANSFERRED TO THE BUYER; but when the property in goods is transferred to the buyer, the goods are AT THE RISK OF THE BUYER whether DELIVERY HAS BEEN MADE OR NOT. EXCEPTIONS: (i) agreement to contrary; (ii) delay in delivery due to fault of a party — risk on that party; (iii) custom of trade; (iv) agreement to separate risk and property.
topic_text: Section 26 — Risk Prima Facie Passes with Property

question_html: The Latin maxim 'Nemo dat quod non habet' in the context of Sale of Goods Act means:

options.A: No buyer can acquire title better than the seller has — a non-owner cannot make valid transfer of property in goods
options.B: The buyer always gets a better title than the seller if he acts in good faith
options.C: The seller's title cannot be challenged once the contract of sale is executed
options.D: The buyer gets absolute title upon payment of price regardless of seller's title

answer_html:
Answer: (B) The buyer always gets a better title than the seller if he acts in good faith

Section 27 / Nemo dat quod non habet: 'NO ONE CAN GIVE WHAT HE HIMSELF DOES NOT HAVE.' A buyer cannot get a GOOD TITLE to goods unless he purchased from the OWNER or someone with owner's AUTHORITY OR CONSENT. If the SELLER'S TITLE IS DEFECTIVE, the BUYER'S TITLE will have the SAME DEFECT. If the seller has NO TITLE, the buyer acquires NO TITLE even if he acted honestly and paid full price. This protects the REAL OWNER of goods. EXCEPTIONS TO NEMO DAT — SECTIONS 27–30
topic_text: Section 27 — Nemo Dat Quod Non Habet

question_html: For the exception of 'sale by a mercantile agent' (Section 27) to apply so that the buyer acquires a good title, which conditions must BOTH be satisfied?

options.A: The agent must be in possession in his capacity as mercantile agent with owner's consent; must sell in ordinary course of business; and the buyer must act in GOOD FAITH WITHOUT NOTICE of lack of authority
options.B: The agent must have a registered power of attorney from the owner
options.C: The agent must provide a written guarantee to the buyer
options.D: The owner must have expressly authorised the specific sale by name

answer_html:
Answer: (C) The agent must provide a written guarantee to the buyer

Exception: Sale by MERCANTILE AGENT — for buyer to acquire GOOD TITLE, ALL these conditions must be met: (1) Person must be in POSSESSION OF GOODS or DOCUMENTS OF TITLE in his CAPACITY AS MERCANTILE AGENT with the CONSENT OF THE OWNER; (2) Must sell while ACTING IN THE ORDINARY COURSE OF BUSINESS; and (3) BUYER MUST ACT IN GOOD FAITH WITHOUT HAVING ANY NOTICE, at the time of contract, that the agent has NO AUTHORITY TO SELL.

question_html: Under Section 28, for the exception of 'sale by a joint owner' to apply, which conditions must be fulfilled?

options.A: One of several joint owners must have SOLE POSSESSION with PERMISSION OF CO-OWNERS; the buyer must purchase in GOOD FAITH; and the buyer should not have NOTICE that the seller has no authority to sell
options.B: All joint owners must collectively consent to the sale
options.C: The joint owner must hold a court order authorising the sale
options.D: The buyer must be a registered mercantile agent

answer_html:
Answer: (A) One of several joint owners must have SOLE POSSESSION with PERMISSION OF CO-OWNERS; the buyer must purchase in GOOD FAITH; and the buyer should not have NOTICE that the seller has no authority to sell

Section 28 Exception (Sale by JOINT OWNER): If there are several joint owners and ONE OF THEM HAS SOLE POSSESSION OF THE GOODS BY PERMISSION OF THE CO-OWNERS, property passes to any person who buys from such joint owner, provided: (1) ONE JOINT OWNER MUST HAVE SOLE POSSESSION; (2) He must have PERMISSION OF CO-OWNERS; (3) BUYER MUST PURCHASE IN GOOD FAITH; and (4) BUYER SHOULD NOT HAVE NOTICE that the seller has no authority to sell.

question_html: Under Section 30(1), a SELLER WHO CONTINUES IN POSSESSION AFTER A SALE may pass a good title to a SUBSEQUENT BUYER if:

options.A: The first buyer was in default in taking delivery
options.B: The subsequent buyer obtains DELIVERY of the goods or documents of title IN GOOD FAITH AND WITHOUT NOTICE of the previous sale
options.C: The seller gets court permission before the second sale
options.D: The subsequent buyer pays a higher price than the first buyer

answer_html:
Answer: (B) The subsequent buyer obtains DELIVERY of the goods or documents of title IN GOOD FAITH AND WITHOUT NOTICE of the previous sale

Section 30(1) Exception (Sale by SELLER IN POSSESSION AFTER SALE): Where a person has SOLD GOODS BUT CONTINUES IN POSSESSION of goods or documents of title, he may sell to a third person. If such third person OBTAINS DELIVERY IN GOOD FAITH AND WITHOUT NOTICE OF THE PREVIOUS SALE, the person acquires a GOOD TITLE to the goods. The seller must be in possession after sale AND there must be delivery or transfer of goods or documents of title by the seller.
topic_text: Exception 5 — Sale by Seller in Possession After Sale

question_html: Under Section 30(2), a buyer who has agreed to buy goods and OBTAINS POSSESSION with consent of the seller may pass a good title to a subsequent buyer. This exception does NOT apply if:

options.A: The buyer pays only a part of the price
options.B: The goods are perishable in nature
options.C: At the time of the subsequent sale, the buyer was NOT IN POSSESSION of the goods or documents
options.D: The seller has not yet received the full price

answer_html:
Answer: (C) At the time of the subsequent sale, the buyer was NOT IN POSSESSION of the goods or documents

Section 30(2) Exception (Sale by BUYER IN POSSESSION AFTER SALE): Where a buyer having bought or agreed to buy goods obtains with CONSENT OF THE SELLER the POSSESSION OF THE GOODS or documents of title, he can resell to a bona fide transferee. DOES NOT APPLY IF: at the time of this sale, THE BUYER WAS NOT IN POSSESSION — the buyer must be in physical possession at the time of the second sale for the exception to protect the sub-buyer.
topic_text: Exception 6 — Sale by Buyer in Possession

question_html: Under Section 29, a person in possession of goods under a VOIDABLE CONTRACT which has NOT BEEN RESCINDED can pass a good title to a buyer if:

options.A: The buyer purchases in GOOD FAITH AND WITHOUT NOTICE of the seller's defective title
options.B: The original owner has been given a reasonable opportunity to object
options.C: The goods have been delivered to the buyer before the contract is rescinded
options.D: The price paid by the buyer is at market value

answer_html:
Answer: (A) The buyer purchases in GOOD FAITH AND WITHOUT NOTICE of the seller's defective title

Section 29 Exception (Sale by PERSON IN POSSESSION UNDER VOIDABLE CONTRACT): A person in possession of goods under a VOIDABLE CONTRACT (induced by fraud, misrepresentation, coercion, undue influence) WHICH HAS NOT YET BEEN RESCINDED, can transfer a GOOD TITLE to the buyer, provided the BUYER PURCHASES IN GOOD FAITH AND WITHOUT NOTICE of the seller's defective title.

question_html: Exception 7 to the nemo dat rule states that if an unpaid seller has EXERCISED RIGHT OF LIEN OR STOPPAGE IN TRANSIT AND RESELLS the goods, the second buyer acquires a good title:

options.A: Only if the resale was justified in the circumstances
options.B: As against the ORIGINAL BUYER — even though the resale may not be justified in the circumstances
options.C: Only if the seller gave notice of resale to the original buyer
options.D: Only if the resale price is lower than the original contract price

answer_html:
Answer: (B) As against the ORIGINAL BUYER — even though the resale may not be justified in the circumstances

Exception 7 (Sale by UNPAID SELLER): If the unpaid seller has EXERCISED RIGHT OF LIEN OR STOPPAGE IN TRANSIT and RESELLS THE GOODS, the SECOND BUYER ACQUIRES A GOOD TITLE AS AGAINST THE ORIGINAL BUYER — EVEN THOUGH THE RESALE IS NOT JUSTIFIED IN THE CIRCUMSTANCES. This protects the bona fide second buyer while the seller's rights against the first buyer remain separate (right to recover deficiency or keep surplus). CONDITIONS & WARRANTIES — SECTIONS 12–17

question_html: Which of the following CORRECTLY states the key legal distinction between a condition and a warranty under Section 12 of the Sale of Goods Act?

options.A: A condition gives right to claim damages only; a warranty gives right to repudiate the contract
options.B: Both condition and warranty give identical remedies — only the name differs
options.C: A CONDITION is essential to the main purpose of the contract (breach allows REPUDIATION); a WARRANTY is collateral to the main purpose (breach gives right to DAMAGES ONLY — not rejection)
options.D: A condition can be waived; a warranty can never be waived

answer_html:
Answer: (C) A CONDITION is essential to the main purpose of the contract (breach allows REPUDIATION); a WARRANTY is collateral to the main purpose (breach gives right to DAMAGES ONLY — not rejection)

Section 12(2): A CONDITION = stipulation ESSENTIAL TO THE MAIN PURPOSE of the contract; breach gives right to TREAT THE CONTRACT AS REPUDIATED. Section 12(3): A WARRANTY = stipulation COLLATERAL TO THE MAIN PURPOSE; breach gives right to claim DAMAGES but NOT to reject goods or treat contract as repudiated. IMPORTANT: A stipulation may be a condition THOUGH CALLED A WARRANTY in the contract — its legal character depends on construction of the contract, not its name.
topic_text: Section 12 — Condition vs Warranty: Core Distinction

question_html: Under Section 13, in which situation is the buyer compelled to treat a BREACH OF CONDITION as a BREACH OF WARRANTY (rather than repudiating the contract)?

options.A: When the buyer expressly waives the condition
options.B: When the contract is not severable AND the buyer has already accepted the goods or part thereof — breach of condition can only be treated as breach of warranty, not a ground for rejecting goods
options.C: When the goods are perishable
options.D: When the price has already been paid in full

answer_html:
Answer: (A) When the buyer expressly waives the condition

Section 13 — Two situations where condition is treated as warranty: (1) The buyer WAIVES THE CONDITION; (2) The contract is NOT SEVERABLE AND THE BUYER HAS ACCEPTED THE GOODS OR PART — the breach of any condition to be fulfilled by the seller can ONLY be treated as a breach of WARRANTY (not a ground for rejecting goods and repudiating the contract). Section 13(3): No remedy when condition fulfilment is excused by law due to impossibility.
topic_text: Section 13 — When Condition Treated as Warranty

question_html: Under Section 14(a), which of the following is an implied condition in every contract of sale?

options.A: That the seller has the right to sell the goods (or will have the right at the time property is to pass in an agreement to sell)
options.B: That the goods are of the highest quality available in the market
options.C: That the seller has a registered title to the goods
options.D: That the buyer must inspect the goods before purchase

answer_html:
Answer: (B) That the goods are of the highest quality available in the market

Section 14(a): IMPLIED CONDITION AS TO TITLE — In a contract of sale, unless circumstances show different intention, there is an implied condition that: (i) in the case of a SALE, the seller HAS A RIGHT TO SELL the goods; and (ii) in the case of an AGREEMENT TO SELL, he WILL HAVE A RIGHT TO SELL the goods at the time when the property is to pass. Rowland v. Divall (1923) is the classic case — a car sold without right to sell entitles buyer to full refund.
topic_text: Section 14(a) — Implied Condition as to Title

question_html: Section 14(b) provides an implied WARRANTY OF QUIET POSSESSION. What does this warranty mean?

options.A: The buyer is guaranteed that the goods will be in a quiet location
options.B: The seller warrants that neither he nor anyone claiming under a superior title or under his authority shall interfere with the QUIET ENJOYMENT of the buyer
options.C: The buyer is entitled to use the goods without any tax liability
options.D: The seller must deliver the goods quietly without any commercial announcement

answer_html:
Answer: (C) The buyer is entitled to use the goods without any tax liability

Section 14(b): WARRANTY OF QUIET POSSESSION — the buyer is entitled to quiet enjoyment of the goods purchased. Neither the SELLER nor anyone CLAIMING UNDER A SUPERIOR TITLE or under the seller's authority shall INTERFERE WITH THE BUYER'S QUIET ENJOYMENT. Section 14(c): WARRANTY OF FREEDOM FROM ENCUMBRANCES — goods are free from any CHARGE OR RIGHT OF ANY THIRD PARTY not declared or known to the buyer before the contract. These are the two key implied warranties.

question_html: Under Section 15, where there is a contract for sale of goods BY DESCRIPTION, which implied condition exists?

options.A: The goods shall correspond with the sample only — not with the description
options.B: The seller shall disclose all defects of the goods before sale
options.C: The goods SHALL CORRESPOND WITH THE DESCRIPTION; and if sale is by sample AS WELL AS by description, it is not sufficient that the bulk corresponds with the sample if the goods do not ALSO CORRESPOND WITH THE DESCRIPTION
options.D: The price shall be determined by the buyer based on the goods received

answer_html:
Answer: (A) The goods shall correspond with the sample only — not with the description

Section 15: Where there is a contract for sale of goods BY DESCRIPTION, there is an IMPLIED CONDITION that the GOODS SHALL CORRESPOND WITH THE DESCRIPTION. If the sale is by SAMPLE AS WELL AS BY DESCRIPTION, it is NOT SUFFICIENT that the BULK CORRESPONDS WITH THE SAMPLE if the goods do NOT ALSO CORRESPOND WITH THE DESCRIPTION. Goods are 'sold by description' when described in the contract and buyer contracted RELYING ON SUCH DESCRIPTION.

question_html: Under Section 17, in a contract for sale BY SAMPLE, which of the following implied conditions exists?

options.A: Only that the bulk shall correspond with the sample in quality
options.B: (i) Bulk shall CORRESPOND WITH SAMPLE IN QUALITY; (ii) buyer shall have a REASONABLE OPPORTUNITY OF COMPARING the bulk with the sample; and (iii) goods shall be FREE FROM ANY DEFECT RENDERING THEM UN-MERCHANTABLE which would not be apparent on REASONABLE EXAMINATION of the sample
options.C: The buyer must pay immediately on delivery of sample
options.D: The seller must keep the sample available for 6 months

answer_html:
Answer: (B) (i) Bulk shall CORRESPOND WITH SAMPLE IN QUALITY; (ii) buyer shall have a REASONABLE OPPORTUNITY OF COMPARING the bulk with the sample; and (iii) goods shall be FREE FROM ANY DEFECT RENDERING THEM UN-MERCHANTABLE which would not be apparent on REASONABLE EXAMINATION of the sample

Section 17: A contract for sale by SAMPLE (where there is a term, express or implied, to that effect) has THREE implied conditions: (i) the BULK SHALL CORRESPOND WITH THE SAMPLE IN QUALITY; (ii) the buyer shall have a REASONABLE OPPORTUNITY OF COMPARING THE BULK WITH THE SAMPLE; (iii) the goods shall be FREE FROM ANY DEFECT RENDERING THEM UN-MERCHANTABLE which would not be APPARENT ON REASONABLE EXAMINATION OF THE SAMPLE (i.e., latent defects).
topic_text: Section 17 — Sale by Sample: Implied Conditions

question_html: The doctrine of Caveat Emptor (embodied in Section 16) means 'let the buyer beware'. What is its PRINCIPAL EFFECT in a contract of sale?

options.A: The seller must disclose all known defects to the buyer before sale
options.B: The buyer must recover all defects before filing a suit
options.C: Subject to the Act, there is NO IMPLIED WARRANTY OR CONDITION as to the QUALITY OR FITNESS FOR ANY PARTICULAR PURPOSE of goods supplied under a contract of sale — it is the buyer's duty to satisfy himself
options.D: The seller bears the risk of any latent defects in the goods

answer_html:
Answer: (C) Subject to the Act, there is NO IMPLIED WARRANTY OR CONDITION as to the QUALITY OR FITNESS FOR ANY PARTICULAR PURPOSE of goods supplied under a contract of sale — it is the buyer's duty to satisfy himself

Section 16: Embodies CAVEAT EMPTOR ('let the buyer beware'): 'SUBJECT TO THE PROVISIONS OF THIS ACT AND OF ANY OTHER LAW, THERE IS NO IMPLIED WARRANTY OR CONDITION AS TO THE QUALITY OR FITNESS FOR ANY PARTICULAR PURPOSE of goods supplied under a contract of sale.' It is NOT the SELLER'S DUTY to give goods fit for the buyer's purpose. Case: Ward v. Hobbs (1878) — pigs sold at auction; no warranty of health; buyer beware. If the buyer makes a wrong selection, he cannot blame the seller.

question_html: Which of the following is a VALID EXCEPTION to the doctrine of Caveat Emptor under Section 16?

options.A: Where the buyer EXPRESSLY OR IMPLIEDLY makes known to the seller the PARTICULAR PURPOSE for which goods are required, showing reliance on seller's skill/judgment, and the goods are of a description the seller supplies — then there is an implied condition that goods shall be REASONABLY FIT FOR SUCH PURPOSE
options.B: Where the buyer inspects the goods personally before purchase
options.C: Where the seller provides a written warranty
options.D: Where the goods are perishable in nature

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Where the buyer EXPRESSLY OR IMPLIEDLY makes known to the seller the PARTICULAR PURPOSE for which goods are required, showing reliance on seller's skill/judgment, and the goods are of a description the seller supplies — then there is an implied condition that goods shall be REASONABLY FIT FOR SUCH PURPOSE

Section 16 Exceptions to Caveat Emptor: (a) Where buyer EXPRESSLY OR IMPLIEDLY makes known the PARTICULAR PURPOSE, showing RELIANCE ON SELLER'S SKILL OR JUDGMENT — IMPLIED CONDITION that goods shall be REASONABLY FIT FOR SUCH PURPOSE. EXCEPTION WITHIN EXCEPTION: no implied condition for goods of a PATENT OR TRADE NAME. (b) Where goods are bought BY DESCRIPTION from a dealer in such goods — implied condition of MERCHANTABLE QUALITY (unless buyer examined and defects would have been apparent). (c) Usage of trade; (d) Express warranty/condition does not negate implied warranty unless inconsistent.

question_html: For the implied condition of 'merchantable quality' under Section 16(2) to apply, which of the following conditions must be satisfied?

options.A: The seller must be a manufacturer of the goods
options.B: The seller should be a dealer in goods of that description AND if the buyer examined the goods, there shall be no implied condition as regards defects which the examination OUGHT TO HAVE REVEALED (but latent defects remain covered)
options.C: The price must exceed Rs. 10,000
options.D: The buyer must place the order in writing

answer_html:
Answer: (B) The seller should be a dealer in goods of that description AND if the buyer examined the goods, there shall be no implied condition as regards defects which the examination OUGHT TO HAVE REVEALED (but latent defects remain covered)

Section 16(2): Implied condition of MERCHANTABLE QUALITY applies when: (i) SELLER IS A DEALER IN GOODS OF THAT DESCRIPTION (whether manufacturer or not); (ii) Goods are BOUGHT BY DESCRIPTION. EXCEPTION: If the BUYER HAS EXAMINED THE GOODS, there shall be NO IMPLIED CONDITION as regards DEFECTS WHICH SUCH EXAMINATION OUGHT TO HAVE REVEALED. For eatables/provisions: additional implied condition that goods shall be WHOLESOME. The term 'merchantability' is not defined in the Act.

question_html: Which of the following correctly states the remedy for BREACH OF WARRANTY under the Sale of Goods Act?

options.A: The buyer can reject the goods and repudiate the contract
options.B: The buyer can reject the goods OR claim damages at his option
options.C: The breach of warranty gives right to claim DAMAGES only; the buyer CANNOT reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated
options.D: The buyer can claim specific performance of the contract

answer_html:
Answer: (C) The breach of warranty gives right to claim DAMAGES only; the buyer CANNOT reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated

Breach of WARRANTY: (a) RIGHT TO CLAIM DAMAGES — but NOT to reject goods or treat the contract as repudiated; (b) Buyer may SET UP the breach in EXTINCTION OR DIMINUTION of the price; (c) Buyer may SUE FOR DAMAGES. No remedy if warranty fulfilment becomes impossible by law. Breach of CONDITION: (a) Reject goods and repudiate contract; (b) Treat it as warranty and claim damages; (c) Once treated as warranty, cannot repudiate; (d) No remedy if excused by impossibility [Section 13(3)]. PERFORMANCE OF CONTRACT OF SALE — SECTIONS 31–44
topic_text: Remedies for Breach of Condition vs Warranty

question_html: Under Section 32, unless otherwise agreed, payment and delivery in a contract of sale are:

options.A: Concurrent conditions — seller must be ready to deliver in exchange for price; buyer must be ready to pay in exchange for possession
options.B: Sequential — payment must always precede delivery
options.C: Sequential — delivery must always precede payment
options.D: Independent obligations — either party may insist on his own right without tendering performance

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Concurrent conditions — seller must be ready to deliver in exchange for price; buyer must be ready to pay in exchange for possession

Section 32: Unless OTHERWISE AGREED, DELIVERY OF GOODS AND PAYMENT OF PRICE ARE CONCURRENT CONDITIONS — the SELLER shall be ready and willing to GIVE POSSESSION OF THE GOODS to the buyer in EXCHANGE FOR THE PRICE; and the BUYER shall be ready and willing to PAY THE PRICE in EXCHANGE FOR POSSESSION OF THE GOODS. Neither party needs to perform unless the other is ready and willing to perform.

question_html: Under Section 37, where the seller delivers a LARGER QUANTITY than contracted, the buyer may:

options.A: Only reject the entire delivery
options.B: Accept the goods included in the contract and reject the rest, OR reject the whole; if he accepts the whole, he pays at the CONTRACT RATE
options.C: Accept all the goods and pay only for the contracted quantity
options.D: Accept the extra goods at no charge as a bonus

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Accept the goods included in the contract and reject the rest, OR reject the whole; if he accepts the whole, he pays at the CONTRACT RATE

Section 37 rules on WRONG QUANTITY: (1) LESS than contracted — buyer may REJECT; if accepted, pays at CONTRACT RATE; (2) MORE than contracted — buyer may ACCEPT CONTRACTED QUANTITY AND REJECT THE REST, or REJECT THE WHOLE; if he accepts THE WHOLE, he pays at CONTRACT RATE; (3) GOODS MIXED WITH DIFFERENT DESCRIPTION — buyer may ACCEPT CONFORMING GOODS AND REJECT THE REST, or REJECT THE WHOLE. All these provisions are subject to usage of trade, special agreement or course of dealing.

question_html: Under Section 39, if the seller is authorised to send goods to the buyer through a carrier and the seller OMITS TO MAKE A REASONABLE CONTRACT with the carrier, and goods are LOST OR DAMAGED in transit, the buyer may:

options.A: Claim insurance from the government
options.B: Sue the carrier only — the seller has no responsibility
options.C: DECLINE TO TREAT DELIVERY TO CARRIER AS DELIVERY TO HIMSELF, or HOLD THE SELLER RESPONSIBLE FOR DAMAGES
options.D: Only claim against the carrier under the Carriers Act

answer_html:
Answer: (C) DECLINE TO TREAT DELIVERY TO CARRIER AS DELIVERY TO HIMSELF, or HOLD THE SELLER RESPONSIBLE FOR DAMAGES

Section 39(2): The SELLER shall make a REASONABLE CONTRACT with the carrier having regard to nature of goods and circumstances. If the seller OMITS TO DO SO and goods are LOST OR DAMAGED in transit or whilst in custody of the wharfinger, the buyer may: (a) DECLINE TO TREAT DELIVERY TO THE CARRIER OR WHARFINGER AS DELIVERY TO HIMSELF; or (b) HOLD THE SELLER RESPONSIBLE FOR DAMAGES. Section 39(3): For SEA TRANSIT — seller must give buyer notice to enable him to insure goods; failure = goods at seller's risk during sea transit.

question_html: Under Section 42, the buyer is deemed to have ACCEPTED the goods in which of the following situations?

options.A: (i) When he intimates acceptance to the seller; OR (ii) when he does any act in relation to goods inconsistent with seller's ownership; OR (iii) when after a reasonable time he retains goods without intimating rejection
options.B: Only when he makes the full payment for the goods
options.C: Only when he uses or consumes the goods
options.D: Only when he signs a receipt acknowledging delivery

answer_html:
Answer: (A) (i) When he intimates acceptance to the seller; OR (ii) when he does any act in relation to goods inconsistent with seller's ownership; OR (iii) when after a reasonable time he retains goods without intimating rejection

Section 42: Buyer is DEEMED TO HAVE ACCEPTED goods when: (a) he INTIMATES TO THE SELLER THAT HE HAS ACCEPTED THEM; (b) the goods are DELIVERED and he does ANY ACT INCONSISTENT WITH THE OWNERSHIP OF THE SELLER (e.g., reselling, mortgaging, using); or (c) after LAPSE OF A REASONABLE TIME, he RETAINS THE GOODS WITHOUT INTIMATING TO THE SELLER THAT HE HAS REJECTED THEM. Section 43: Where buyer REJECTS goods, he is NOT BOUND TO RETURN THEM — sufficient to INTIMATE rejection to seller.
topic_text: Section 42 — When Buyer is Deemed to Have Accepted Goods

question_html: Under Section 41, the buyer has a right to EXAMINE goods before acceptance. The purpose of this examination is:

options.A: To negotiate a lower price after finding defects
options.B: To ascertain whether the goods are in CONFORMITY WITH THE CONTRACT; the seller is also bound to AFFORD AN OPPORTUNITY for examination
options.C: To determine if he wants to return the goods
options.D: Only to verify the quantity, not the quality

answer_html:
Answer: (B) To ascertain whether the goods are in CONFORMITY WITH THE CONTRACT; the seller is also bound to AFFORD AN OPPORTUNITY for examination

Section 41: The buyer has a RIGHT TO EXAMINE the goods which have NOT been examined by him PREVIOUSLY BEFORE ACCEPTANCE. The examination is FOR THE PURPOSE OF ASCERTAINING WHETHER THEY ARE IN CONFORMITY WITH THE CONTRACT. The SELLER IS ALSO BOUND TO AFFORD AN OPPORTUNITY to the buyer for examining the goods for the same purpose. This right is different from the right of rejection — examination precedes and informs acceptance.

question_html: Under Section 44, where the seller is READY AND WILLING TO DELIVER but the buyer NEGLECTS OR REFUSES TO TAKE DELIVERY within a reasonable time, the buyer is liable for:

options.A: Only a penalty equal to 10% of the contract price
options.B: Damages only — no additional charges
options.C: Any LOSS OCCASIONED BY HIS NEGLECT OR REFUSAL, and also for a REASONABLE CHARGE FOR CARE AND CUSTODY of the goods
options.D: The full contract price as a penalty

answer_html:
Answer: (C) Any LOSS OCCASIONED BY HIS NEGLECT OR REFUSAL, and also for a REASONABLE CHARGE FOR CARE AND CUSTODY of the goods

Section 44: Where the seller is READY AND WILLING TO DELIVER and REQUESTS the buyer to take delivery, and the buyer does not within a REASONABLE TIME take delivery, the buyer is liable for: (a) any LOSS OCCASIONED BY HIS NEGLECT OR REFUSAL to take delivery; and (b) also for a REASONABLE CHARGE FOR THE CARE AND CUSTODY of the goods. The rights of the seller shall NOT BE AFFECTED where such neglect/refusal amounts to a REPUDIATION OF THE CONTRACT. RIGHTS OF UNPAID SELLER — SECTIONS 45–61
topic_text: Section 44 — Buyer's Liability for Not Taking Delivery

question_html: Under Section 45(1), a seller is deemed an 'UNPAID SELLER' when:

options.A: The whole of the price has NOT been paid or tendered; OR a bill of exchange/negotiable instrument was received as conditional payment but its condition has not been fulfilled (e.g., dishonour)
options.B: Only when the price has not been paid at all and there is no negotiable instrument
options.C: Only when the buyer becomes formally declared insolvent by a court
options.D: When the seller has not yet delivered the goods

answer_html:
Answer: (A) The whole of the price has NOT been paid or tendered; OR a bill of exchange/negotiable instrument was received as conditional payment but its condition has not been fulfilled (e.g., dishonour)

Section 45(1): Seller is an UNPAID SELLER when: (a) the WHOLE OF THE PRICE HAS NOT BEEN PAID OR TENDERED; OR (b) when a BILL OF EXCHANGE OR OTHER NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENT has been received as CONDITIONAL PAYMENT and the CONDITION HAS NOT BEEN FULFILLED by reason of DISHONOUR OF THE INSTRUMENT OR OTHERWISE. Section 45(2): 'Seller' includes any person in the POSITION OF A SELLER — e.g., an AGENT OF THE SELLER to whom the bill of lading has been endorsed, or a CONSIGNOR or AGENT who has himself paid or is directly responsible for the price.

question_html: Under Sections 47-49, an unpaid seller in POSSESSION of goods may exercise his RIGHT OF LIEN (retain goods) in which of the following situations?

options.A: Only where the buyer has been formally adjudicated as insolvent by a court
options.B: Where goods are sold WITHOUT STIPULATION AS TO CREDIT; OR goods are sold on credit but CREDIT TERM HAS EXPIRED; OR the BUYER BECOMES INSOLVENT
options.C: Where the seller chooses not to deliver the goods
options.D: Where the delivery address is in a different city

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Where goods are sold WITHOUT STIPULATION AS TO CREDIT; OR goods are sold on credit but CREDIT TERM HAS EXPIRED; OR the BUYER BECOMES INSOLVENT

Sections 47-49: An UNPAID SELLER IN POSSESSION may exercise LIEN (keep goods and refuse delivery until price is paid or tendered) where: (a) goods were sold WITH NO STIPULATION AS TO CREDIT (cash sale); (b) goods sold on CREDIT but CREDIT TERM HAS EXPIRED; or (c) BUYER BECOMES INSOLVENT. The LIEN IS POSSESSORY — exercisable only while seller IS IN POSSESSION. It can only be exercised for NON-PAYMENT OF PRICE, not for other charges.

question_html: An unpaid seller LOSES his RIGHT OF LIEN in which of the following situations?

options.A: Only when the buyer pays the full price
options.B: Only when a court order is obtained by the buyer
options.C: (a) When seller delivers goods to a carrier for transmission to buyer WITHOUT RESERVING RIGHT OF DISPOSAL; (b) when buyer or his agent LAWFULLY OBTAINS POSSESSION; (c) by WAIVER OF LIEN by the seller
options.D: When the goods are sold on credit for more than 6 months

answer_html:
Answer: (C) (a) When seller delivers goods to a carrier for transmission to buyer WITHOUT RESERVING RIGHT OF DISPOSAL; (b) when buyer or his agent LAWFULLY OBTAINS POSSESSION; (c) by WAIVER OF LIEN by the seller

LIEN IS LOST when: (a) the seller DELIVERS GOODS TO A CARRIER OR BAILEE for transmission to the buyer WITHOUT RESERVING THE RIGHT OF DISPOSAL; (b) the BUYER OR HIS AGENT LAWFULLY OBTAINS POSSESSION of the goods; (c) by WAIVER OF HIS LIEN by the unpaid seller. The lien depends on PHYSICAL POSSESSION — once possession is lost (other than through waiver), the lien is lost. The seller's lien is NOT affected by any sub-sale by the buyer UNLESS the seller ASSENTED to it.

question_html: The RIGHT OF STOPPAGE IN TRANSIT is available to an unpaid seller under which conditions?

options.A: When the buyer is insolvent (need not be court-declared) AND the goods are still in transit
options.B: Only when the buyer has been formally adjudicated insolvent by a court and goods are in transit
options.C: Any time before the goods reach the buyer's premises
options.D: Only when the bill of lading has not been endorsed to the buyer

answer_html:
Answer: (A) When the buyer is insolvent (need not be court-declared) AND the goods are still in transit

Sections 50-52: RIGHT OF STOPPAGE IN TRANSIT = right to stop goods while in transit, resume possession, and retain possession until payment or tender. Available when: (1) BUYER BECOMES INSOLVENT — need not be FORMALLY DECLARED INSOLVENT by court; it is sufficient if he HAS CEASED TO PAY DEBTS IN ORDINARY COURSE OF BUSINESS or CANNOT PAY DEBTS AS THEY BECOME DUE; AND (2) GOODS ARE IN TRANSIT (from delivery to carrier until buyer takes delivery).

question_html: Under Section 51, in which of the following situations does the TRANSIT COME TO AN END?

options.A: When the goods reach the halfway point of their journey
options.B: (a) If buyer obtains delivery BEFORE ARRIVAL AT DESTINATION; (b) if after arrival at destination, CARRIER ACKNOWLEDGES to buyer that he holds goods on buyer's behalf; (c) if carrier WRONGFULLY REFUSES TO DELIVER goods to buyer
options.C: Only when the goods physically arrive at the buyer's premises
options.D: When the seller gives notice of stoppage to the carrier

answer_html:
Answer: (B) (a) If buyer obtains delivery BEFORE ARRIVAL AT DESTINATION; (b) if after arrival at destination, CARRIER ACKNOWLEDGES to buyer that he holds goods on buyer's behalf; (c) if carrier WRONGFULLY REFUSES TO DELIVER goods to buyer
